order-counted (conceptual): The 11 elements were counted in order (¹²P₁₁); a subset has no order, so it is ¹²C₁₁.
one-per-element (conceptual): Only the 12 subsets of the form {a} and {a, x} were counted; a can be joined by any subset of the other 11 elements.

teach.idea: Building a subset means deciding, for each element, in or out: two choices per element, so a set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, including ∅ and the set itself.
teach.method: Count all subsets as 2ⁿ, then remove what the question excludes: A itself for proper subsets, ∅ as well for non-empty proper subsets. Subsets of a fixed size r are ⁿCᵣ.

alternatives.title: List a small case
text: For {a, b}: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b} — four subsets, 2².
Adding an element c doubles the list: every old subset, and every old subset with c added.

families.title: Counting with n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
explanations: only-part (conceptual): n(A ∪ B) − n(B) (or n(A ∪ B) − n(A)) was given; that counts the elements in only one of the sets, not those in both.
common-not-removed (conceptual): n(A) was given; A − B leaves out the elements of A that are also in B.
wrong-set (procedural): n(A ∪ B) − n(A) was found; that is n(B − A), not n(A − B).
common-twice (conceptual): n(A) and n(B) were added; the 26 common elements are then counted twice, once in each set.
common-removed-twice (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was taken away twice; it is counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so it is taken away once.
intersection-given (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was found and given; take it away from n(A) to get n(A − B).

teach.idea: When n(A) and n(B) are added, the elements in both sets are counted twice, so n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
teach.method: Write the formula, put in the three numbers you know and solve for the fourth. For 'A only', take n(A ∩ B) away from n(A).

alternatives.title: Fill the Venn regions from the middle
text: Write n(A ∩ B) in the overlap first.
Then A only = n(A) − overlap and B only = n(B) − overlap; the union is the three regions added.

families.title: Counting elements of A × B and relations from A to B
explanations: added (conceptual): n(A) and n(B) were added; each of the 6 elements of A pairs with each of the 6 elements of B, so they multiply.
pairs-not-subsets (conceptual): The number of ordered pairs was given; a relation is any subset of A × B, and a set of mn pairs has 2^(mn) subsets.
power-of-sum (procedural): 2 was raised to n(A) + n(B); A × B has 6 × 2 = 12 pairs, so the count is 2^12.
empty-relation-left-out (conceptual): The empty relation was left out; ∅ is a subset of A × B, so it is a relation too.
subtracted (conceptual): n(A) was subtracted from n(A × B); n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B), so divide by 6.

teach.idea: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B, so n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B). A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B.
teach.method: Multiply the sizes for the product. For the number of relations, raise 2 to the power n(A) × n(B).

alternatives.title: Draw the pairs as a grid
text: Write A down the side and B along the top: each cell is one ordered pair.
The grid has n(A) rows and n(B) columns; a relation is a choice of cells to tick.

families.title: Is a relation reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
explanations: some-diagonal (conceptual): Some pairs (a, a) are in R, so R was called reflexive; reflexive needs every one of (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3).
transitive-a-equals-c (conceptual): Chains that come back to the start were skipped: (1, 2) and (2, 1) in R need (1, 1) in R too.
chain-missed (procedural): A chain was missed: (1, 3) and (3, 1) are in R, but (1, 1) is not.
some-pairs-checked (procedural): Only some pairs were checked for symmetry; every (a, b) in R needs its partner (b, a) in R.

teach.idea: Reflexive: every element is related to itself. Symmetric: whenever (a, b) is in R, so is (b, a). Transitive: whenever (a, b) and (b, c) are in R, so is (a, c) — including chains with a = c.
teach.method: Check each property against the list, one pair or one chain at a time. A single missing pair is enough to say 'not'.

alternatives.title: Write R as a 3 × 3 table
text: Put a 1 in row a, column b when (a, b) is in R.

Reflexive: 1s all along the diagonal. Symmetric: the table equals its mirror image across the diagonal. Transitive: whenever row a has a 1 in column b and row b has a 1 in column c, row a has a 1 in column c.

families.title: The domain of a real function
explanations: end-left-out (procedural): x = −3/2 was left out; √0 = 0 is a real number, so the end point belongs to the domain.
sign-not-reversed (conceptual): Both sides were divided by −1 without reversing the inequality; dividing by a negative number reverses it.
b-sign (procedural): 9 was moved across without changing its sign.
root-rule-used (conceptual): The quadratic was made positive, as under a square root; a denominator only has to be non-zero, so just x = a and x = b are removed.
root-signs (procedural): The roots were read with the wrong signs: x² − 11x + 30 = (x − 5)(x − 6) is zero at x = 5 and x = 6.
sign-region (conceptual): The interval between the roots was chosen; the quadratic is negative there.
ends-left-out (procedural): The roots were left out; √0 = 0 is defined.
denominator-zero (conceptual): The roots 5 and 6 were included; there the denominator is √0 = 0.
minus-ignored (conceptual): The minus sign in front of x² was ignored; −x² + 11x − 30 = (x − 5)(6 − x) is ≥ 0 between the roots.

teach.idea: The domain of a real function is every real x for which the formula gives a real number: what is under a square root must be ≥ 0, and a denominator must not be 0.
teach.method: Write the condition (≥ 0, > 0 or ≠ 0), factorise any quadratic, decide the sign of each region between the roots, and write the answer in interval notation.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Mark the roots on a number line; they cut it into regions.
Pick one number in each region and find the sign of the quadratic there; keep the regions that meet the condition, and decide each end point separately.

alternatives.title: Test numbers in f
text: Try a few values of x in the formula: if you need the square root of a negative number, or divide by zero, x is not in the domain.
The boundary values are where the quantity is exactly 0: test them separately.

families.title: The range of a quadratic function
explanations: f-at-zero (conceptual): f(0) = 84 was taken as the least value; the extreme value is at the vertex, x = 5.
direction (conceptual): The parabola was taken to open the other way; with a positive x² coefficient f has a least value.
end-open (procedural): 9 was left out; f(5) = 9, so it is in the range.
x-for-y (conceptual): The x-coordinate of the vertex (5) was used; the range is about the values of f, so use f(5).
vertex-sign (procedural): The vertex was put at x = −5; it is at x = −b/(2a) = 5.

teach.idea: Writing f(x) = a(x − h)² + k shows the range: (x − h)² takes every value ≥ 0, so f takes every value from k upwards when a > 0, and from k downwards when a < 0.
teach.method: Complete the square (or find the vertex at x = −b/(2a)), work out k = f(h), and write [k, ∞) or (−∞, k].

alternatives.title: Use the vertex formula
text: For ax² + bx + c the vertex is at x = −b/(2a).
Substitute it to get the least (a > 0) or greatest (a < 0) value; the range is the ray from there.

families.title: Is a function one-one, onto, both or neither?
explanations: codomain-as-range (conceptual): Onto was assumed; on [0, ∞) f only reaches values from 4 upwards, not every real number.
positive-x-only (conceptual): Only x ≥ 0 was tried; f(−1) = f(1), so on ℝ two inputs share an output.
square-never-one-one (conceptual): x² was taken as never one-one; on [0, ∞) there are no negative inputs, so different inputs give different outputs.
pair-missed (conceptual): f(−x) = f(x) was missed: on ℝ, f(−1) = f(1), so f is not one-one.
cube-like-square (conceptual): x³ was treated like x²; (−x)³ = −x³, so a cube takes every real value exactly once.

teach.idea: One-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) only when x₁ = x₂. Onto: every element of the codomain is f(x) for some x in the domain. Both depend on the domain and codomain, not only on the formula.
teach.method: For one-one, look for two different inputs with the same output (for x², try x and −x). For onto, find the range on the given domain and compare it with the codomain.

alternatives.title: Horizontal lines on the graph
text: Sketch the graph over the given domain only.
One-one: no horizontal line meets it twice. Onto: every horizontal line at a height in the codomain meets it at least once.

families.title: A point on a transformed graph
explanations: shift-direction (conceptual): The graph was moved the wrong way; f(−5 − x) takes the value f(5) when x = −10.
stretch-after-shift (procedural): 1 was added to 5 before multiplying by 2; in y = 2f(−5 − x) + 1 the value of f is multiplied by 2 first, and then 1 is added.
reflection-forgotten (conceptual): The −x inside f was ignored; it reflects the graph in the y-axis, so the x-coordinate changes sign before the shift.

teach.idea: In y = a·f(x − h) + v, the graph moves h to the right, is stretched by a (reflected if a < 0) and moves v up. A point (p, q) goes to (p + h, aq + v); f(h − x) also reflects it in the line x = h.
teach.method: Find the x that makes the input of f equal to p, then work out the output: multiply q by a, then add v.

alternatives.title: Track one point in a table
text: Write three columns: x, the input to f, and y.
Choose x so the input is p; then f gives q, and the outside numbers turn q into y.

families.title: Evaluating the greatest integer function
explanations: drop-decimals (conceptual): The decimal part was simply removed; for a negative number that moves up, but [x] is the integer at or below x: [−2.3] = −3.
nearest (conceptual): The numbers were rounded to the nearest integer; [x] always goes down to the integer at or below x.
ceiling (recall): The integer above was taken; the greatest integer function takes the integer at or below x.

teach.idea: [x] is the greatest integer that is not more than x: on the number line it is the integer at x or the first one to its left. So [2.7] = 2 but [−2.7] = −3.
teach.method: Place each number on the number line and step left to the nearest integer (stay if it is already an integer), then add or subtract.

alternatives.title: Step left on the number line
text: Mark the number between two integers.
The greatest integer function always takes the left-hand one, even for negative numbers.

families.title: The corner point of a feasible region off the axes
explanations: intercepts-combined (conceptual): The smaller x-intercept and the smaller y-intercept were put together; the corner off the axes is where the two lines cross, found by solving them together.
swapped (procedural): The coordinates were written the wrong way round; give the x value first.

teach.idea: Each constraint ≤ is a half-plane bounded by a line; the corner points of the feasible region are where two boundary lines meet inside the region.
teach.method: Replace ≤ by = in the two constraints and solve the pair of equations (by elimination); check the point satisfies x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

alternatives.title: Eliminate one variable
text: Multiply the equations so that the y terms have the same coefficient, and subtract to find x.
Put x back into either equation to find y.

families.title: Solving |ax + b| = c
explanations: one-case (conceptual): Only 6x + 12 = 15 was solved; the modulus is also 15 when 6x + 12 = −15.
second-case-sign (procedural): In the second case the sign of 12 was lost: −(6x + 12) = 15 gives 6x + 12 = −15.
b-sign (procedural): 12 was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: |A| is the distance of A from 0, so |A| = c (with c > 0) means A = c or A = −c: two equations.
teach.method: Write the two cases ax + b = c and ax + b = −c, and solve each.

alternatives.title: Distance on the number line
text: |ax + b| = c says ax is at distance c from −b.
Step c units left and right of −b to find the two values of ax, then divide by a.

families.title: Solving |ax + b| < c, ≤ c, > c, ≥ c
explanations: wrong-region (conceptual): The inside was chosen; |6x + 12| ≥ 4 means 6x + 12 is more than 4 from 0, on either side.
one-side (conceptual): Only 6x + 12 ≥ 4 was solved; the modulus also counts the negative side.
end-points (procedural): The end points were left out; with ≥ they belong to the answer.
b-sign (procedural): 12 was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: |A| < c means A is within c of 0: −c < A < c. |A| > c means A is further than c from 0: A < −c or A > c.
teach.method: Rewrite without the modulus (one double inequality, or two inequalities joined by 'or'), solve for x, and write the answer in interval notation with the right brackets.

alternatives.title: Distance from a point
text: |ax + b| is the distance between ax and −b on the number line.
'Less than c' is the stretch of length 2c centred at −b; 'more than c' is everything outside it.

families.title: Solving a quadratic inequality
explanations: leading-sign (conceptual): The negative x² coefficient was ignored; −(x − 7)(x − 8) is positive between the roots and negative outside.
end-points (procedural): The roots were included; there the expression is 0, which does not satisfy a strict inequality.
root-signs (procedural): The roots were read with the wrong signs; the expression is zero at x = 7 and x = 8.
wrong-region (conceptual): The wrong region was chosen; (x − 6)(x − 8) is negative between 6 and 8 and positive outside.

teach.idea: A quadratic with roots a < b keeps one sign between the roots and the other sign outside them; the sign outside is the sign of the x² coefficient.
teach.method: Factorise, mark the roots on a number line, find the sign in each region, keep the regions the inequality asks for, and include the roots only for ≤ or ≥.

alternatives.title: Picture the parabola
text: With a positive x² coefficient the parabola opens upwards: it is below the x-axis only between the roots.
With a negative coefficient it opens downwards: it is above the x-axis only between the roots.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Write the sign of each factor in each region.
Multiply the signs (and the sign of the leading number) to get the sign of the product.

families.title: Solving a rational inequality (x − a)/(x − b) compared with 0
explanations: multiplied-out (conceptual): Both sides were multiplied by x − 6 as if it were positive; its sign changes at x = 6, so compare signs of top and bottom instead.
wrong-region (conceptual): The wrong region was chosen; the fraction is negative between 6 and 8, where top and bottom have opposite signs.
denominator-zero (conceptual): x = 6 was included; there the denominator is 0 and the fraction is not defined.

teach.idea: A fraction is positive when top and bottom have the same sign and negative when they differ; it is 0 where the top is 0 and undefined where the bottom is 0.
teach.method: Mark the zeros of the top and of the bottom, find the sign of the fraction in each region, and keep the regions asked for. The zero of the bottom is always left out.

alternatives.title: Same sign as the product
text: (x − a)/(x − b) has the same sign as (x − a)(x − b) wherever x ≠ b.
Solve the product inequality, then remove x = b.

families.title: Partial fractions with two distinct linear factors
explanations: cover-up-sign (procedural): In the cover-up step the other factor was worked out the wrong way round: at x = 5 the factor x − 6 is −1, not 1.
not-divided (procedural): The numerator's value was not divided by the value of the other factor.
swapped (procedural): A and B were swapped; A goes with x − 5, found by putting x = 5.

teach.idea: (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) means px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a) for every x, so choosing x = a and x = b each removes one unknown.
teach.method: Factorise the denominator, multiply through, then put x = a to find A and x = b to find B. Check at one more value of x.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Expand A(x − b) + B(x − a) = (A + B)x − (Ab + Ba).
Match the x coefficient and the constant with px + q and solve the two equations for A and B.

families.title: Partial fractions with a linear and an irreducible quadratic factor
explanations: not-divided (procedural): N(5) was taken as A without dividing by 5² + 9 = 34.
x2-as-B (procedural): B was taken as the whole x² coefficient 2; the x² terms come from A·x² and Bx·x, so B = 2 − A.
c-sign (procedural): A sign slip matching the x terms: (Bx + C)(x − 5) gives (C − 5B)x.

teach.idea: A quadratic factor x² + k with no real roots needs a linear numerator Bx + C. Multiplying out, N(x) = A(x² + k) + (Bx + C)(x − a) holds for every x.
teach.method: Put x = a to find A. Then compare the x² coefficients to find B and the x (or constant) terms to find C.

alternatives.title: Three equations
text: Expand the right side and match the x², x and constant coefficients with N(x).
This gives three equations in A, B and C; solve them together.

families.title: Permutations of r out of n distinct objects
explanations: order-ignored (conceptual): The objects were chosen without order (¹⁵C₈); in an arrangement the order matters.
repetition (conceptual): Every place was given all 15 choices; an object used in one place cannot be used again, so the choices go down by one each time.
all-arranged (procedural): All 13 objects were arranged (13!); only 9 places are filled.
divide-by-r (recall): 13! was divided by 9!; ¹³P₉ = 13!/(13 − 9)!.

teach.idea: Filling r places in order from n distinct objects: n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on, so ⁿPᵣ = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1) = n!/(n − r)!.
teach.method: Multiply r numbers, starting at n and going down by one each time.

alternatives.title: Draw the places as boxes
text: Draw r boxes in a row and write in each how many objects are still free to go there.
By the multiplication principle, multiply the numbers in the boxes.

families.title: Combinations: choosing r out of n
explanations: order-counted (conceptual): The 10 objects were counted in order (²⁰P₁₀); a selection has no order, so divide by 10!.
multiply-n-r (conceptual): 20 and 18 were multiplied; count the ordered choices 20 × 19 × … and divide by 18!.
divide-by-r-not-factorial (recall): ²⁰P₁₁ was divided by 11; each selection of 11 can be arranged in 11! ways, so divide by 11!.

teach.idea: Choosing without order: each group of r objects appears r! times among the ordered arrangements, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ / r! = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
teach.method: Use the smaller of r and n − r (ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ), multiply that many numbers down from n, and divide by its factorial.

alternatives.title: Pascal's triangle
text: Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it; row n, place r (counting from 0) is ⁿCᵣ.
This is because a choice of r from n either includes a particular object or not: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁻¹Cᵣ₋₁ + ⁿ⁻¹Cᵣ.

families.title: Selections with a condition: exactly k from one group
explanations: added (conceptual): The two choices were added; each choice of women goes with each choice of men, so multiply.
condition-ignored (conceptual): 6 were chosen from all 17 people; the condition fixes exactly 5 women and 1 man.
order-counted (conceptual): The members were arranged in order; a committee is a selection, so use combinations.

teach.idea: A condition splits the selection into independent parts: choose the women, choose the men, and multiply (every choice of one goes with every choice of the other).
teach.method: Work out ʷCₖ for the women and ᵐCᵣ₋ₖ for the men, then multiply.

alternatives.title: List a tiny case
text: With 2 women and 2 men, a committee of 2 with exactly 1 woman: 2 choices of woman × 2 choices of man = 4 committees.
Listing them shows each woman paired with each man.

families.title: Arrangements when some objects are identical
explanations: identical-as-distinct (conceptual): All 11 letters were treated as different (11!); swapping two equal letters gives the same arrangement.
counts-not-factorials (recall): The total was divided by the group sizes; divide by their factorials (the ways each group can be shuffled).
one-group-only (procedural): Only the largest group of equal letters was divided out; divide by the factorial of every group.

teach.idea: If all n objects were different there would be n! arrangements; each arrangement of identical objects is counted p! × q! × … times, once for every shuffle of equal objects.
teach.method: Work out n! and divide by the factorial of the size of each group of identical objects.

alternatives.title: Choose places for each colour
text: Choose the places for the first colour (ⁿCₚ), then for the second colour from the places left, and so on.
Multiply the choices: this gives the same number as n!/(p! q! …).

families.title: A coefficient in the expansion of (ax + b)ⁿ
explanations: powers-left-out (conceptual): Only ⁸C₇ was given; the term also carries (3x)⁷ and (3)¹, so their powers are part of the coefficient.
general-term-index (procedural): The general term was used with the wrong index: the term with x⁷ uses ⁸C₇ and the powers 7 and 1.
a-power-forgotten (procedural): The 3 in (3x)⁷ was not raised to the power 7.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was dropped; a negative number to an odd power is negative.

teach.idea: The general term of (u + v)ⁿ is ⁿCᵣ uʳ vⁿ⁻ʳ. With u = ax and v = b, the term with xʳ is ⁿCᵣ aʳ bⁿ⁻ʳ xʳ.
teach.method: Pick the term whose power of x is r, then multiply ⁿCᵣ by aʳ and by bⁿ⁻ʳ, keeping the signs.

alternatives.title: Read the row of Pascal's triangle
text: Row n of Pascal's triangle gives ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, … ⁿCₙ.
Each one multiplies a power of ax and a power of b whose powers add up to n.

families.title: Expanding (ax + b)ⁿ
explanations: ends-only (conceptual): Only the first and last terms were written; (3x + 5)⁴ is not 81x⁴ + 625 — there are 5 terms.
no-binomial-coefficients (procedural): The binomial coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 were left out.
signs-lost (procedural): The signs were lost; odd powers of −1 are negative, so the signs alternate.

teach.idea: (u + v)ⁿ = ⁿC₀uⁿ + ⁿC₁uⁿ⁻¹v + … + ⁿCₙvⁿ: the power of u goes down while the power of v goes up, and the coefficients are a row of Pascal's triangle.
teach.method: Write the row of Pascal's triangle for n, then each term ⁿCᵣ (ax)ⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, and simplify each coefficient with its sign.

alternatives.title: Multiply step by step
text: (ax + b)² = a²x² + 2abx + b²; multiply by (ax + b) again for the cube, and so on.
This shows where the Pascal numbers come from: each new row adds neighbours.

families.title: The term independent of x in (xᵖ ± k/x^q)ⁿ
explanations: k-power-forgotten (procedural): Only ¹²C₆ was given; the term also carries (3)⁶ from k/x³.
sign-lost (procedural): (−1)⁵ is negative, since 5 is odd.
middle-term (conceptual): The middle term was taken; the constant term is where the powers of x cancel, which need not be the middle.
q-ignored (procedural): The power of x in the denominator was taken as 1; 1/x³ contributes x^(−3r).

teach.idea: In (xᵖ + k/x^q)ⁿ the general term is ⁿCᵣ (xᵖ)ⁿ⁻ʳ (k/x^q)ʳ = ⁿCᵣ kʳ x^(p(n − r) − qr). The term independent of x is the one whose power of x is 0.
teach.method: Write the power of x in the general term, set it equal to 0 to find r, then work out ⁿCᵣ kʳ.

alternatives.title: List the powers of x
text: Write the power of x in each term for r = 0, 1, 2, …: it goes down by p + q each time.
The term where the power reaches 0 is the constant term.

families.title: The nth term of a geometric progression
explanations: power-n (procedural): r was raised to the power 10; the 10th term is a r^9, because the first term has no factor r.
arithmetic (conceptual): The common difference was used as in an AP; each term here is 3 times the one before.
ar-power (procedural): (ar)^7 was worked out; only r is raised to the power, then multiply by a.

teach.idea: In a GP each term is the one before times r, so going from the 1st to the nth term multiplies by r exactly n − 1 times: aₙ = a r^(n − 1).
teach.method: Find r by dividing the second term by the first, then work out a r^(n − 1), keeping track of the sign.

alternatives.title: Keep multiplying
text: Write the terms out, multiplying by r each time, until you reach the term asked for.
Count the multiplications: one fewer than the term's position.

families.title: The sum of the first n terms of a GP
explanations: last-term (conceptual): The 7th term was found; the question asks for the sum of all 7 terms.
one-term-short (procedural): r^6 was used in the formula; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) uses r^7.
divide-by-r (recall): The formula was divided by r; it is divided by r − 1.

teach.idea: Sₙ = a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹. Multiplying by r shifts every term along one place, so rSₙ − Sₙ = arⁿ − a and Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
teach.method: Find a and r, then put them in Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), working out rⁿ with its sign first.

alternatives.title: Add the terms
text: For a few terms, list them and add.
Check that the formula gives the same total — then trust it for many terms.

families.title: The sum to infinity of a geometric series
explanations: plus-r (procedural): 1 + r was used; the sum to infinity is a/(1 − r), with r = 2/5.
a-left-out (procedural): The first term was left out; the sum is a/(1 − r), not 1/(1 − r).
first-terms-only (conceptual): Only the terms shown were added; the series goes on for ever, and the sum to infinity adds all of them.

teach.idea: When |r| < 1 the terms shrink towards 0 and the partial sums a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) approach a/(1 − r), because rⁿ → 0.
teach.method: Find r = second term ÷ first term, check |r| < 1, and work out a/(1 − r).

alternatives.title: Watch the partial sums
text: Add 1, 2, 3, 4 … terms and write each total down.
The totals get closer and closer to one number: that number is the sum to infinity.

families.title: The sum to infinity of an arithmetico-geometric series
explanations: gp-only (conceptual): Only the geometric part was summed, as if every coefficient were the first one; the coefficients grow by d each time.
one-minus-r-once (procedural): After subtracting rS from S, the result was not divided by 1 − r again.
d-without-r (procedural): The shifted series was taken to start with d instead of dr.

teach.idea: In an AGP the coefficients form an AP and the powers of r a GP. Subtracting rS from S lines up equal powers of r, and the differences of the AP are all d, leaving a GP.
teach.method: Write S and rS one place apart, subtract to get S(1 − r) = a + dr + dr² + ⋯ = a + dr/(1 − r), then divide by 1 − r.

alternatives.title: Use the formula
text: Check it by adding the first few terms: the totals approach your answer.

families.title: The harmonic mean of two numbers
explanations: arithmetic-mean (conceptual): The arithmetic mean was found; the harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the mean of the reciprocals.
not-inverted (procedural): The mean of the reciprocals was found but not turned back over.
geometric-mean (conceptual): The geometric mean √(ab) was found; the harmonic mean is 2ab/(a + b).

teach.idea: Numbers are in harmonic progression when their reciprocals are in AP. The harmonic mean H of a and b is the middle one: 1/H is the average of 1/a and 1/b, so H = 2ab/(a + b).
teach.method: Add the reciprocals, halve, and turn the result upside down — or use 2ab/(a + b) directly.

alternatives.title: Compare the three means
text: For positive a ≠ b, AM > GM > HM, and GM² = AM × HM.
So the harmonic mean should come out smaller than (a + b)/2 — a quick check.

families.title: Using the laws of logarithms: log N in terms of log 2 and log 3
explanations: five-as-sum (conceptual): log 5 was taken as log 2 + log 3, because 2 + 3 = 5; logs turn products into sums, and 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so log 5 = 1 − a.
decimal-ignored (procedural): The decimal point was ignored; 518.4 is a whole number divided by 10, which subtracts 1.
powers-not-multiplied (procedural): A power was not brought down: log 2³ = 3 log 2 = 3a, not a.

teach.idea: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y and log xⁿ = n log x. With log 10 = 1, log 5 = log(10/2) = 1 − log 2.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of powers of 2, 3 and 5 (a decimal is a whole number over a power of 10), take logs term by term, and replace log 5 by 1 − a.

alternatives.title: Check with a calculator
text: Put these into your answer: it should match log of the number to four decimal places.

families.title: Evaluating a logarithm by writing both numbers as powers of one base
explanations: upside-down (conceptual): The exponents were divided the wrong way; log₆₂₅ x asks which power of 625 gives x, so it is 5/4.
subtract-exponents (procedural): The powers were subtracted; the logarithm is the power that turns the base into the number, here a quotient of the powers.
sign-lost (procedural): 1/5 = 5^-1: the power is negative.
divide-numbers (conceptual): 3125 was divided by 625; a logarithm is a power, not a quotient of the numbers.

teach.idea: log_B X = y means Bʸ = X. If B = cⁱ and X = cʲ, then (cⁱ)ʸ = cʲ, so iy = j and y = j/i.
teach.method: Write the base and the number as powers of the same prime, then divide the power of the number by the power of the base.

alternatives.title: Change of base
text: log_B X = log_c X / log_c B.
With X = cʲ and B = cⁱ this is j/i.

families.title: Solving log x + log(x ± c) = k
explanations: extraneous-kept (conceptual): The negative root was kept; log of a negative number is not defined, so x = −1000 is rejected.
sum-inside (conceptual): log x + log(x + 999) was taken as log(2x + 999); the sum of logs is the log of the product, x(x + 999).

teach.idea: log x + log y = log(xy), and log_B N = k means N = Bᵏ. A logarithm is only defined for positive numbers, so every root must be checked.
teach.method: Combine the logs into one, rewrite as x(x ± c) = Bᵏ, solve the quadratic, and keep only roots that make both x and x ± c positive.

alternatives.title: Substitute each root
text: Put each root back into the original equation.
If any logarithm would have a zero or negative number inside, that root is not a solution.

families.title: Solving a quadratic with negative discriminant over ℂ
explanations: q-not-divided (procedural): √(164) was not divided by 2a = 6; the whole of −b ± √(b² − 4ac) is divided by 2a.
p-sign (procedural): The real part was taken as b/(2a); it is −b/(2a) = −4/3.
half-only (procedural): The imaginary part was divided by 2 only; divide by 2a = 6.

teach.idea: The quadratic formula works over ℂ: when b² − 4ac < 0, √(b² − 4ac) = i√(4ac − b²), so the roots are −b/(2a) ± i√(4ac − b²)/(2a), a conjugate pair.
teach.method: Find D = b² − 4ac, write √D = i√(−D) and simplify the surd, then divide both −b and √(−D) by 2a.

alternatives.title: Complete the square
text: Divide by a and write (x + b/(2a))² = (b² − 4ac)/(4a²), a negative number.
Take square roots using i: x + b/(2a) = ± i√(4ac − b²)/(2a).

families.title: A real quadratic from one complex root
explanations: sum-sign (procedural): p was taken as k × (sum of roots); the sum of the roots is −p/k, so p = −3 × 12 = −36.
i-squared (recall): (6 + 6i)(6 − 6i) was worked out with i² = +1; since i² = −1 the product is a² + b² = 72.
k-forgotten (procedural): The leading coefficient 3 was forgotten; the quadratic is 3(x² − (sum)x + product).

teach.idea: A polynomial with real coefficients has its non-real roots in conjugate pairs: if a + bi is a root, so is a − bi. Their sum is 2a and their product is a² + b².
teach.method: Write the quadratic as k(x² − (sum)x + product) and read off p and q.

alternatives.title: Substitute and match parts
text: Put x = a + bi into kx² + px + q and expand, using i² = −1.
The real part and the imaginary part must both be 0: two equations for p and q.

families.title: Inserting arithmetic means between two numbers
explanations: divide-by-k (conceptual): The difference 62 − 20 was split into 5 equal parts; 5 means make 6 gaps between 20 and 62.
count-ends-as-gaps (procedural): The difference was split into 7 parts, as if the two given numbers were gaps too; there are 7 terms but only 6 gaps.
ends-listed (procedural): The two given numbers were listed as well; the means are only the numbers in between.

teach.idea: Inserting k arithmetic means between a and b makes an arithmetic progression of k + 2 terms with a first and b last, so b = a + (k + 1)d.
teach.method: Find d = (b − a)/(k + 1), then add d to a again and again to get the k means.

alternatives.title: Equal jumps on a number line
text: Mark a and b on a number line. The k means cut the distance into k + 1 equal jumps.
One jump is (b − a)/(k + 1); jump from a to get each mean.

families.title: Inserting geometric means between two numbers
explanations: arithmetic-means (conceptual): Equal differences were used; geometric means go up (or down) by the same FACTOR, not the same amount.
ends-listed (procedural): The two given numbers were listed as well; the means are only the numbers in between.
root-k (procedural): The ratio was found as the square root of 9/576; with 2 means there are 3 steps, so it is the cube root.

teach.idea: Inserting k geometric means between a and b makes a geometric progression of k + 2 terms, so b = a·r^(k + 1).
teach.method: Find r = (b/a)^(1/(k + 1)) (the positive root, since the means are positive), then multiply a by r again and again.

alternatives.title: The powers of r form an AP
text: The terms are a·r⁰, a·r¹, …, a·r^(k + 1): the powers 0, 1, …, k + 1 are equally spaced.
So b/a is r to the power (number of steps); try r = 2, 3, … until r^(k + 1) = b/a.

families.title: The least value of ax + b/x by AM ≥ GM
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): Only the GM √(360) was given; AM ≥ GM says (ax + b/x)/2 ≥ √(ab), so the sum itself is at least 2√(ab).
gave-x (procedural): The value of x where the least value happens (x = √(b/a)) was given, not the least value of the expression.
x-is-one (conceptual): x = 1 was put in; the least value is where the two terms are equal (ax = b/x), not at x = 1.

teach.idea: For positive p and q, (p + q)/2 ≥ √(pq), with equality exactly when p = q. Here p = ax and q = b/x have a fixed product ab.
teach.method: Multiply the two terms: (ax)(b/x) = ab. So ax + b/x ≥ 2√(ab), and the value 2√(ab) is reached when ax = b/x, i.e. x = √(b/a).

alternatives.title: Complete the square
text: A square is never negative, so the least value is 2√(ab), when the square is 0.

families.title: A coefficient in the binomial series for a rational index
explanations: power-of-k-left-out (procedural): The coefficient of yʳ in (1 + y)ⁿ was given, but y = 3x, so it must be multiplied by (3)³.
rising-factors (conceptual): The factors were taken as n(n + 1)(n + 2)…; the general term uses n(n − 1)(n − 2)… even when n is negative or a fraction.
no-factorial (recall): The product n(n − 1)… was not divided by 3!.
sign-of-k (procedural): The minus sign in 1 − x was dropped; (−1)³ is negative for an odd power.

teach.idea: For any rational n and |y| < 1, (1 + y)ⁿ = 1 + ny + n(n − 1)y²/2! + n(n − 1)(n − 2)y³/3! + …; when n is not a whole number the series never stops.
teach.method: The coefficient of yʳ is n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1)/r!. Put y = kx, so the coefficient of xʳ is that number times kʳ (keep the sign of k).

alternatives.title: Write out the first terms
text: Write 1 + n(kx) + [n(n − 1)/2](kx)² + [n(n − 1)(n − 2)/6](kx)³ with your n and k.
Simplify each bracket, then read off the term you need.

families.title: A coefficient in the exponential or logarithmic series
explanations: no-factorial (recall): The term was not divided by 5!; e^y = 1 + y + y²/2! + y³/3! + …
k-not-raised (procedural): The 4/3 inside was not raised to the power 5: the term is (4/3x)⁵.
divide-by-r (recall): The term was divided by 5, as in the log series; the exponential series divides by 5! = 120.
signs-not-alternating (recall): Every term of log(1 + y) was taken as positive; the signs alternate: y − y²/2 + y³/3 − …
factorial-for-log (recall): The term was divided by 5!; in the log series it is divided by 5 (the exponential series has the factorials).

teach.idea: eʸ = 1 + y + y²/2! + y³/3! + … for every y, and log(1 + y) = y − y²/2 + y³/3 − … for |y| < 1.
teach.method: Put y = kx. The coefficient of xʳ is kʳ/r! for eᵏˣ, and (−1)^(r + 1) kʳ/r for log(1 + kx).

alternatives.title: Where the log series comes from
text: d/dy log(1 + y) = 1/(1 + y) = 1 − y + y² − … (a geometric series).
Integrating term by term gives y − y²/2 + y³/3 − …, so the divisors are 1, 2, 3, … and the signs alternate.

families.title: The general term of a sequence from its first terms
explanations: n-not-n-minus-1 (procedural): aₙ = a + nd was used; the first term has no d added, so aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
d-left-out (conceptual): The common difference 9 was not used as the coefficient of n; each step adds 9, so aₙ has 9n.
first-term-times-n (conceptual): The first term was multiplied by n; that would make every term a multiple of 18.
treated-as-ap (conceptual): Only the first difference was used, as if the sequence were an AP; here the differences themselves change, so aₙ has an n² term.
whole-second-difference (procedural): The coefficient of n² was taken as the second difference (2); it is half of it, because n² itself has second difference 2.
square-only (procedural): Only n² was matched to the first term; the n term is needed too (check a₂ and a₃).

teach.idea: A general term is a rule that gives aₙ straight from n. If the differences are constant (d), aₙ = dn + (a₁ − d); if the second differences are a constant 2, aₙ = n² + bn + c.
teach.method: Write the differences. Constant: the coefficient of n is d, then fix the constant from a₁. Second differences 2: write n² + bn + c and find b and c from a₁ and a₂.

alternatives.title: Test your rule
text: Put n = 1, 2, 3 into your rule and compare with the given terms.
If a₁ fits but a₂ does not, the coefficient of n is wrong; if all are off by the same number, the constant is wrong.

families.title: Writing an arithmetic series in sigma notation
explanations: no-shift (procedural): The k-th term was taken as a + kd; with k starting at 1 that skips the first term. It is a + (k − 1)d.
start-at-zero (procedural): k was started at 0 but still run to 12; that gives 13 terms.
one-short (conceptual): The upper limit was taken one too small; it is the number of terms, 12.
last-term-as-limit (conceptual): The last term was used as the upper limit; the upper limit counts the terms (12).

teach.idea: Σ (k = 1 to m) t(k) means t(1) + t(2) + … + t(m): the limits count the terms and the expression t(k) gives each one.
teach.method: Find the k-th term (for an AP, a + (k − 1)d), take the number of terms as the upper limit, and check by putting k = 1 and k = m.

alternatives.title: Expand each option
text: For each option write the terms for the lowest and highest k, and count how many values k takes.
The right option starts with the first term, ends with the last term and has the right number of terms.

families.title: A telescoping sum
explanations: wrong-last-term (procedural): The last fraction left after cancelling was taken as 1/122; that one cancels. The one left over is 1/126.
added-parts (procedural): The two remaining fractions were added; they come from a − sign in each partial fraction, so they are subtracted.
factor-left-out (procedural): The factor 1/4 from the partial fractions was left out: 1/((4k + …)(4k + … + 4)) = (1/4)[… − …].

teach.idea: If each term is a difference f(k) − f(k + 1), then in the sum all the middle parts cancel and only f(1) − f(n + 1) is left.
teach.method: Split 1/((dk + e)(dk + e + d)) into (1/d)[1/(dk + e) − 1/(dk + e + d)], write the first two and last terms to see the cancelling, and keep the first and the last fraction.

alternatives.title: Spot the pattern in partial sums
text: For 1/(k(k + 1)) the sums of 1, 2, 3 terms are 1/2, 2/3, 3/4.
The pattern n/(n + 1) is exactly 1 − 1/(n + 1): the first part minus the last part.

families.title: A sum using the standard sums of k, k² and k³
explanations: constant-once (conceptual): The constant 1 was added only once; Σ (k = 1 to 6) 1 adds it 6 times, giving 6.
square-of-sum (recall): Σk² was taken as (Σk)²; that is the rule for Σk³. Σk² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
one-short (procedural): The sum was stopped at k = 5; k runs up to 6.
cubes-over-two (recall): Σk³ was taken as n²(n + 1)²/2; it is [n(n + 1)/2]² = n²(n + 1)²/4.

teach.idea: Σ is linear: Σ(a·f(k) + b·g(k)) = aΣf(k) + bΣg(k), and the sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
teach.method: Split into Σk³, Σk², Σk and Σ1, use [n(n + 1)/2]², n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, n(n + 1)/2 and n, then combine with the coefficients.

alternatives.title: Check with a small case
text: Put n = 2 into your working and compare with adding the first two terms by hand.
If they disagree, check the constant term (it is added n times) and which formula you used for each power.

families.title: Counting the elements of Cartesian products
explanations: upper-end-included (procedural): The end 8 was counted in A, but x < 8 leaves it out; A has 6 elements.
added (conceptual): The numbers of elements were added; each choice from A goes with each choice from B and from C, so they multiply.
third-added (procedural): n(A × B) was found, then n(C) was added; A × B × C has a triple for every pair and every element of C.
pairs-not-subsets (conceptual): n(A × B) = 10 was given; a relation is any subset of A × B, and a set with 10 elements has 2^10 subsets.
functions-counted (conceptual): The number of functions from A to B (2^5) was found; every subset of A × B is a relation, not only the functions.
power-of-sum (procedural): 2^(5 + 2) was used; the exponent is n(A × B) = 5 × 2.
union (conceptual): The union (A × B) ∪ (A × C) was counted; the intersection keeps only pairs whose second entry is in both B and C.
forgot-a (procedural): Only B ∩ C was counted; each of its 4 elements pairs with each of the 6 elements of A.

teach.idea: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Each of the n(A) first entries goes with each of the n(B) second entries, so n(A × B) = n(A)·n(B).
teach.method: Count each set first (list it if it is in set-builder form), then multiply. A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B, so there are 2^(n(A)·n(B)) of them.

alternatives.title: A grid of pairs
text: Draw a grid with a row for each element of A and a column for each element of B.
Each cell is one ordered pair, so the number of cells is rows × columns.

families.title: Reading the sets from a Cartesian product
explanations: swapped (conceptual): The first entries were read; B is made of the SECOND entries of the pairs in A × B.
all-numbers (procedural): Every number in the pairs was listed; only one position of each pair belongs to this set.

teach.idea: In A × B every pair has its first entry from A and its second entry from B, and every combination appears.
teach.method: To find A, collect the first entries of the pairs, writing each value once; to find B, collect the second entries.

alternatives.title: Put the pairs in a table
text: Make a table with one row for each different first entry and one column for each different second entry.
The row labels form A and the column labels form B.

families.title: Intersection, union and difference of intervals
explanations: reversed-difference (conceptual): B − A was found; A − B keeps the numbers of A that are NOT in B.
brackets-of-b-kept (procedural): B's own brackets were copied at the cut; when B is removed, an end that B includes is left OUT of A − B, and an end B leaves out stays IN.
ends-all-closed (procedural): Every end was written with a square bracket; check each end: is that number itself in the set?
intersection-instead (conceptual): The intersection was found; A ∪ B keeps every number that is in EITHER interval.
union-instead (conceptual): The union was found; A ∩ B keeps only the numbers that are in BOTH intervals.

teach.idea: An interval is a set of real numbers. A ∩ B keeps the numbers in both, A ∪ B the numbers in either, and A − B the numbers of A that are not in B. A square bracket includes its end; a round one leaves it out.
teach.method: Draw both intervals on one number line, shade what the operation keeps, then read off the ends, deciding for each end whether that number itself is in the result.

alternatives.title: Test points on the number line
text: Mark all four ends. Test one number in each gap and each end itself: is it in A? in B?
Keep the points the operation wants and join them into intervals.

families.title: Solving a double linear inequality
explanations: middle-only (procedural): 9 was taken away from the middle only; whatever is done to the middle must be done to all three parts.
both-included (procedural): Both ends were included; only the end that comes from ≤ belongs to the solution set.

teach.idea: A double inequality is two inequalities at once; do the same thing to all three parts. Dividing by a negative number reverses both signs, so the left and right ends swap places.
teach.method: Subtract b from all three parts, divide all three by a (reversing the signs if a < 0), rewrite with the smaller number on the left, and use [ ] for ≤ and ( ) for <.

alternatives.title: Split into two inequalities
text: Solve p < ax + b and ax + b ≤ q separately.
The solution set is where both hold: the overlap of the two answers on a number line.

families.title: Matching a set of real numbers with its interval notation
explanations: strict-or-not (conceptual): Strict and non-strict were mixed up: > or < gives a round bracket, ≥ or ≤ a square one.
direction (conceptual): The direction was reversed: x > 6 means numbers to the right of 6, up to ∞.
brackets-swapped (conceptual): Square and round brackets were swapped: [ ] means the end IS included (≤), ( ) means it is not (<).
one-end-read (procedural): Only one end was checked; decide separately for the left end and for the right end whether it is included.

teach.idea: [ or ] means the end belongs to the set (≤, ≥); ( or ) means it does not (<, >). ∞ always gets a round bracket because it is not a real number.
teach.method: Look at each end on its own: is that number in the set? Then write the smaller end on the left and the larger on the right.

alternatives.title: Filled and open dots
text: On a number line a filled dot is an included end ([ ]) and an open dot an excluded end (( )).
Draw the set, then translate each dot into a bracket.

families.title: The inverse of a linear or fractional linear function
explanations: reciprocal (conceptual): f⁻¹ was taken as 1/f(x); the inverse UNDOES f (f⁻¹(f(x)) = x), it is not the reciprocal.
sign-slip (procedural): A sign was lost when the x terms were collected on one side; check by putting your answer into f.
undo-wrong-order (procedural): The steps were undone in the wrong order: f multiplies by 5 first and then adds 5, so f⁻¹ first takes away 5 and then divides by 5.
sign-of-b (procedural): 5 was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: f⁻¹ undoes f: y = f(x) exactly when x = f⁻¹(y). It exists because f is one-one and onto its codomain.
teach.method: Write y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y (for a fraction, multiply up and collect the x terms), then rename y as x.

alternatives.title: Check by composing
text: Pick a number, say x = 1, and work out f(1).
Put f(1) into your f⁻¹: you must get 1 back. Try a second number to be sure.

families.title: A value of an inverse function
explanations: f-not-inverse (conceptual): f(1) was worked out; f⁻¹(1) is the x for which f(x) = 1.
reciprocal (conceptual): 1/f(1) was given; f⁻¹ is the inverse function, not the reciprocal.
sign-slip (procedural): A sign was lost when the x terms were collected; check by putting your answer into f.

teach.idea: f⁻¹(t) is the number x with f(x) = t: the inverse runs the function backwards.
teach.method: Set (ax + b)/(cx + d) = t, multiply both sides by cx + d, collect the x terms and divide.

alternatives.title: Find f⁻¹(x) first
text: Find the formula f⁻¹(x) = (b − dx)/(cx − a).
Then put x = t into it.

families.title: Maximising by the corner-point method
explanations: infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was used as a corner; every corner must satisfy ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): Only the point where the two lines meet was checked; Z must be worked out at every corner of the feasible region.

teach.idea: A linear objective takes its greatest and least values over a bounded feasible region at corner points of the region.
teach.method: Draw each constraint line, find the corner points (axis intercepts and where lines meet) that satisfy every constraint, work out Z at each, and take the greatest.

alternatives.title: Slide the objective line
text: Draw px + qy = k for a small k and slide it outwards, keeping it parallel.
The last point of the region it touches gives the maximum.

families.title: Minimising over an unbounded feasible region
explanations: origin (conceptual): The origin was used as a corner; (0, 0) does not satisfy the ≥ constraints, so it is not in the feasible region.
infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was used; every corner must satisfy ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): Only the point where the two lines meet was checked; Z must be worked out at every corner.

teach.idea: With ≥ constraints the feasible region is unbounded, but if p, q > 0 then Z = px + qy still has a least value, at a corner point.
teach.method: Find the corner points (the intercepts that satisfy both constraints, and the meeting point), work out Z at each and take the least. For an unbounded region, check that the half-plane px + qy < (that value) has no point in common with the region.

alternatives.title: Slide the cost line inwards
text: Draw px + qy = k for a large k and slide it towards the origin.
The last point of the region it touches gives the minimum.

families.title: The optimal corner point of a linear programme
explanations: infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was chosen; check every corner in ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): The meeting point of the two lines was chosen without comparing Z at the other corners.

teach.idea: The optimal solution is the feasible point where Z is best; for a linear Z it is a corner point of the feasible region.
teach.method: List the corner points that satisfy every constraint, work out Z at each, and choose the corner with the greatest Z.

alternatives.title: A corner table
text: Make a table: corner point, then the value of Z.
Cross out any point that breaks a constraint before comparing.

families.title: Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices
explanations: entry-by-entry (conceptual): Matching entries were multiplied; in a matrix product each entry is a row of A times a column of B, added up.
order-reversed (conceptual): BA was found; matrix multiplication is not commutative, and AB uses the rows of A with the columns of B.
row-by-row (procedural): Rows of A were multiplied with rows of B; use the COLUMNS of B.

teach.idea: Entry (i, j) of AB combines row i of A with column j of B: multiply matching entries and add. In general AB ≠ BA.
teach.method: For each of the four entries take a row of A and a column of B, multiply pairwise and add; keep the signs.

alternatives.title: Column by column
text: Column j of AB is A times column j of B.
So find A[e, g] and A[f, h] (as column vectors) and stand them side by side.

families.title: Solving a matrix equation kX ± A = B
explanations: not-divided (procedural): B + A is 4X, not X; every entry must still be divided by 4.
sign-of-a (procedural): A was moved to the other side without changing its sign: 4X = B + A.

teach.idea: Matrices are equal when every pair of matching entries is equal, so a matrix equation is solved like a number equation, entry by entry.
teach.method: Move A to the other side (subtract it, or add it if it was subtracted), then divide every entry by k.

alternatives.title: Four small equations
text: Write X = [[p, q], [r, s]] and compare entries: k·p ± a₁₁ = b₁₁, and so on.
Solve each of the four equations for one unknown.

families.title: A matrix product as a total bill
explanations: item-left-out (procedural): The third item was left out; a row of 3 quantities times a column of 3 prices has 3 products to add.
added (conceptual): Each quantity was added to its price; the bill multiplies each quantity by its price and then adds.
rows-swapped (procedural): The two rows were written in the wrong order; row 1 of QP comes from row 1 of Q.

teach.idea: A row of quantities times a column of prices is a bill: each quantity is multiplied by its own price and the products are added. QP does this for every row at once.
teach.method: Check the orders: (2 × 3)(3 × 1) gives 2 × 1. For each row of Q, multiply the three entries by the three prices and add.

alternatives.title: Write it as two bills
text: Write each shop's bill as quantity × price + quantity × price + quantity × price.
The two totals, one under the other, are the column matrix QP.

families.title: Solving three equations by X = A⁻¹B
explanations: cofactors-not-transposed (procedural): The matrix of cofactors was used instead of its transpose; adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix.
det-sign (procedural): |A| was found with the wrong sign; check the signs in the expansion (+, −, + along the first row).
not-divided (procedural): adj A · B was not divided by |A|; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|.

teach.idea: A system AX = B with |A| ≠ 0 has exactly one solution, X = A⁻¹B, and A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
teach.method: Find |A|; find the nine cofactors and transpose them to get adj A; multiply adj A by B and divide by |A|.

alternatives.title: Cramer's rule
text: x = |A₁|/|A|, y = |A₂|/|A|, z = |A₃|/|A|, where Aᵢ is A with column i replaced by B.
Check by substituting the values back into each equation.

families.title: Solving two equations with an inverse matrix
explanations: adj-signs (procedural): In the adjoint the off-diagonal entries were not negated; for [[a, b], [c, d]] the adjoint is [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
swapped (procedural): x and y were written the wrong way round; X = [[x], [y]], so the first entry of A⁻¹B is x.
not-divided (procedural): adj A · B was not divided by |A|; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|.

teach.idea: If |A| ≠ 0 then A has an inverse and AX = B gives X = A⁻¹B. For a 2 × 2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/|A|)[[d, −b], [−c, a]].
teach.method: Find |A| = ad − bc, write the adjoint (swap a and d, negate b and c), multiply it by B and divide by |A|.

alternatives.title: Check in both equations
text: Put your x and y into the first equation, then the second.
Both totals must match B; if one does not, look again at the adjoint's signs.

families.title: A cubic whose roots are in progression
explanations: sign-of-sum (recall): The product of the roots was taken with the wrong sign; for ax³ + bx² + cx + d it is −d/a.
middle-only (procedural): Only the middle root was found; divide by (x − middle root) and solve the quadratic left over for the other two.

teach.idea: Roots in AP can be written a − d, a, a + d: their sum is 3a. Roots in GP can be written a/r, a, ar: their product is a³. Vieta then gives the middle root.
teach.method: For an AP, a = (−b/leading coefficient)/3; for a GP, a³ = −(constant)/(leading coefficient). Check a is a root, divide by (x − a) and solve the quadratic.

alternatives.title: Synthetic division
text: Once the middle root a is known, divide the coefficients by a in a synthetic-division table.
The bottom row gives the quadratic; factorise it for the other two roots.

families.title: Solving a cubic with the rational root theorem
explanations: leading-coefficient-ignored (procedural): The root 5/3 was given as 5: a factor of the leading coefficient 3 belongs in the denominator.
signs-reversed (recall): All the signs were reversed; if x − s is a factor then x = s (not −s) is a root.

teach.idea: If p/q (in lowest terms) is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.
teach.method: List the possible p/q, test them (whole numbers first), divide by the factor you find and solve the quadratic that is left.

alternatives.title: Quick tests first
text: If the coefficients add to 0, x = 1 is a root; if p(−1) = 0, x = −1 is a root.
Each root found lowers the degree by one.

families.title: A cubic equation from a volume
explanations: longest-edge (procedural): x + 9 (the longest edge) was given; the question asks for x.
cube-root (conceptual): The cube root of 4536 was taken as if all three edges were equal; the other edges are longer than x, so x is less than ∛4536.

teach.idea: x(x + a)(x + b) = V expands to a cubic with one sign change, so it has exactly one positive root; a whole-number root divides the constant term V.
teach.method: Estimate: x is a little less than ∛V. Test the divisors of V near that estimate until one gives V.

alternatives.title: A trial table
text: Make a table of x and x(x + a)(x + b) for x = 1, 2, 3, …
The volume grows as x grows, so stop when you reach V.

families.title: Finding the other roots from a surd root
explanations: both-signs-changed (conceptual): Both parts of the root changed sign; the conjugate of 4 + √7 changes only the sign of the surd: 4 − √7.
rational-part-changed (conceptual): The sign of the whole-number part was changed; it is the surd part whose sign changes.
sum-sign (recall): The sum of the roots was taken as +(coefficient of x²); it is −(coefficient of x²).

teach.idea: If a polynomial has rational coefficients and u + √w is a root (√w irrational), then its conjugate u − √w is a root too.
teach.method: Multiply (x − (u + √w))(x − (u − √w)) = x² − 2ux + (u² − w), divide the cubic by this quadratic, and read the third root from the linear factor left over.

alternatives.title: Use the sum of the roots
text: The three roots add up to −(coefficient of x²).
The two conjugate roots add up to 2u, so the third root is −(coefficient of x²) − 2u.

families.title: Descartes' rule of signs
explanations: negatives-counted (conceptual): The number of negative coefficients was counted; the rule counts the CHANGES of sign from one non-zero coefficient to the next.
p-not-p-of-minus-x (procedural): The sign changes of p(x) were counted; negative roots need p(−x), where the odd powers change sign.
zeros-as-changes (procedural): Missing terms (zero coefficients) were counted as sign changes; skip the zero coefficients and compare the non-zero ones.

teach.idea: The number of positive roots of p(x) = 0 is at most the number of sign changes in its coefficients (and differs from it by an even number). For negative roots, count the changes in p(−x).
teach.method: Write the signs of the non-zero coefficients in order, skipping zeros, and count the changes. For p(−x), first change the sign of each odd-power coefficient.

alternatives.title: A row of signs
text: Under each power x⁵, x⁴, …, x⁰ write + or − (leave a gap for a missing power).
Draw a mark between each neighbouring pair of signs that differ; count the marks.

families.title: Symmetric functions of the roots of a cubic
explanations: product-sign (recall): αβγ was taken as +d/a; for a cubic it is −d/a.
pair-term-missing (procedural): The expansion missed the αβ + βγ + γα terms: (α + 1)(β + 1)(γ + 1) = αβγ + Σαβ + Σα + 1.
pair-sum-sign (procedural): (α + β + γ)² = Σα² + 2Σαβ, so Σα² = (Σα)² − 2Σαβ; the 2Σαβ was added instead of subtracted.
square-of-sum (conceptual): Σα² was taken as (Σα)²; squaring the sum also gives the cross terms 2(αβ + βγ + γα).
reciprocal-of-sum (conceptual): 1/(α + β + γ) was found; the sum of reciprocals is (αβ + βγ + γα)/αβγ.

teach.idea: For ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 with roots α, β, γ: α + β + γ = −b/a, αβ + βγ + γα = c/a and αβγ = −d/a.
teach.method: Rewrite the expression using only these three sums (e.g. α² + β² + γ² = (Σα)² − 2Σαβ, 1/α + 1/β + 1/γ = Σαβ/αβγ), then substitute.

alternatives.title: The signs alternate
text: Divide by a: x³ − (Σα)x² + (Σαβ)x − αβγ.
So the signs go −, +, − as you move along the coefficients.

families.title: Forming a quadratic with transformed roots
explanations: k-not-squared (procedural): The product was multiplied by −2; (−2α)(−2β) = 4αβ.
sum-sign (recall): The x coefficient was written as +(sum of roots); it is −(sum of roots).
wrong-direction (procedural): The shift went the wrong way: if y = α − 1, the new sum is (α + β) − 2.
identity-sign (procedural): α² + β² was taken as (α + β)² + 2αβ; it is (α + β)² − 2αβ.
product-not-squared (procedural): The product α²β² was taken as αβ; it is (αβ)².

teach.idea: A quadratic with leading coefficient 1 and zeros r₁, r₂ is x² − (r₁ + r₂)x + r₁r₂. For x² + px + q, α + β = −p and αβ = q.
teach.method: Write the new sum and product in terms of α + β and αβ (e.g. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ), substitute, and write x² − (sum)x + (product).

alternatives.title: Substitute for x
text: If y = α + k then α = y − k: put x = y − k into x² + px + q = 0 and expand.
If y = kα, put x = y/k and multiply through by k² to clear the fractions.

families.title: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
explanations: adjoint-only (procedural): The adjoint was given; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|, so every entry must be divided by −24.
no-negation (procedural): a and d were swapped but b and c were not negated; adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
wrong-swap (procedural): The wrong pair was swapped: a and d change places, b and c only change sign.
determinant-added (prerequisite): The determinant was found as ad + bc; it is ad − bc.

teach.idea: A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A, and it exists only when |A| ≠ 0. For [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
teach.method: Find |A| = ad − bc; swap a and d, change the signs of b and c; divide every entry by |A|.

alternatives.title: Row-reduce [A | I]
text: Write A and I side by side and use row operations to turn A into I.
The same operations turn I into A⁻¹; check that AA⁻¹ = I.

families.title: The adjoint of a 3 × 3 matrix
explanations: not-transposed (procedural): The matrix of cofactors was given; adj A is its TRANSPOSE (rows become columns).
no-signs (procedural): The minors were used without the signs (−1)^(i + j); the cofactor of a position with i + j odd is minus its minor.

teach.idea: adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, and A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I, so A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| when |A| ≠ 0.
teach.method: For each entry find its minor (the 2 × 2 determinant left when its row and column are deleted), attach the sign (−1)^(i + j), then transpose the whole matrix.

alternatives.title: Check with A(adj A)
text: Multiply A by your adj A: every off-diagonal entry must be 0.
The diagonal entries must all equal |A|.

families.title: The rank of a 3 × 4 matrix
explanations: rows-counted (conceptual): The non-zero rows of the matrix as given were counted; first reduce it: one row is a combination of the other two, so it becomes a zero row.
one-row-removed (procedural): Only one row was reduced to zero; the third row is also a multiple of the first.
columns-counted (conceptual): The number of columns was taken; the rank is at most the number of rows (3) and is the number of non-zero rows in echelon form.

teach.idea: The rank is the number of non-zero rows in an echelon form: the number of rows that are not combinations of the others.
teach.method: Use row operations (swap rows, Rᵢ → Rᵢ − kRⱼ) to make zeros below each leading entry, then count the rows that are not all zero.

alternatives.title: The largest non-zero minor
text: The rank is the order of the largest square sub-matrix with a non-zero determinant.
Try the 3 × 3 minors (leave out one column at a time); if all are 0, try 2 × 2 minors.

families.title: Deciding the number of solutions of a 3 × 3 system by ranks
explanations: equal-ranks-infinite (conceptual): Equal ranks were read as 'infinitely many solutions'. Equal ranks mean the system is consistent; the solution is unique when that rank equals the number of unknowns (3).
rank-less-none (conceptual): ρ(A) < 3 was read as 'no solution'. When ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) < 3 the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions.
equal-ranks-unique (conceptual): Equal ranks were taken to mean one solution; one solution needs the common rank to be 3, the number of unknowns.
singular-infinite (conceptual): ρ(A) = 2 was taken to mean infinitely many solutions without comparing with ρ([A | B]). Here the augmented matrix has rank 3, so the system is inconsistent.

teach.idea: AX = B is consistent exactly when ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]). If that common rank equals the number of unknowns there is one solution; if it is smaller there are infinitely many.
teach.method: Write [A | B], reduce it to echelon form with row operations, count the non-zero rows of A and of [A | B], and compare them with each other and with 3.

alternatives.title: Determinant first
text: Find |A|. If |A| ≠ 0 the system has exactly one solution.
If |A| = 0, replace each column of A by B in turn: if any of these determinants is non-zero there is no solution; here (with ρ(A) = 2) if all are zero there are infinitely many.

families.title: Finding the parameter values that make a system singular or consistent
explanations: copy-row (conceptual): λ was chosen to copy the z-coefficient of the second equation; the third row must be the same combination of the first two rows in every column.
homogeneous-zero (conceptual): μ = 0 was chosen, as for a homogeneous system; here the third equation must be the same combination of the first two on the right side too.
just-add (procedural): The first two equations were simply added; the third row is 1R₁ − 1R₂, so the right side must be 1 × 1 − 1 × 5.
cofactor-sign (procedural): The determinant was expanded with a + sign on the middle term; the signs along a row are +, −, +.

teach.idea: A unique solution needs |A| ≠ 0. When |A| = 0 the third row is a combination of the other two; the system is consistent (infinitely many solutions) only if the right sides follow the same combination.
teach.method: For λ: expand |A| (it is linear in λ) and solve |A| = 0. For μ: find m, k with R₃ = mR₁ + kR₂ from the x and y columns, then μ = m b₁ + k b₂.

alternatives.title: Row-reduce with the letters
text: Row-reduce [A | B] keeping λ and μ as letters.
The last row becomes (0 0 λ − λ₀ | μ − μ₀): λ = λ₀ removes the pivot, and then μ = μ₀ makes the row all zeros.

families.title: Writing a 3 × 3 matrix as a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric matrix
explanations: wrong-order (procedural): A′ − A was used; Q = ½(A − A′). The other order gives −Q.
not-halved (procedural): A + A′ was not halved: P = ½(A + A′), so that P + Q gives back A.
transpose-as-symmetric (conceptual): A′ was given as the symmetric part; A′ is just A with rows and columns swapped, and is not symmetric unless A is.

teach.idea: (A + A′)′ = A′ + A, so ½(A + A′) is symmetric; (A − A′)′ = −(A − A′), so ½(A − A′) is skew-symmetric. Their sum is A.
teach.method: Write A′, add (for P) or subtract (for Q) entry by entry, and halve. Check: Q has zeros on its diagonal and P + Q = A.

alternatives.title: Average each pair
text: Look at a pair of entries in mirror positions, aᵢⱼ and aⱼᵢ.
P gets their average in both places; Q gets half their difference, with opposite signs in the two places.

families.title: The transpose of a product of 2 × 2 matrices
explanations: same-order (conceptual): A′B′ was found; the transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′.
no-transpose (procedural): AB was found but not transposed; swap its rows and columns.

teach.idea: Transposing swaps rows with columns, and for a product it reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′. (The sizes only fit in that order for non-square matrices.)
teach.method: Either find AB and transpose it, or transpose each matrix and multiply B′ by A′; both give the same matrix.

alternatives.title: Follow one entry
text: The (i, j) entry of (AB)′ is the (j, i) entry of AB: row j of A times column i of B.
That is column j of A′ times row i of B′, which is the (i, j) entry of B′A′.

families.title: The identity element and inverses for a binary operation
explanations: identity-zero (conceptual): 6 ∗ b = 0 was solved; the identity of ∗ is −9, not 0.
identity-sign (procedural): a + e + 9 = a gives e = − 9; the sign was slipped.
negative (conceptual): −3 (the inverse for ordinary addition) was given; the inverse b must satisfy 3 ∗ b = e for this operation's identity e.
identity-one (conceptual): 3 ∗ b = 1 was solved; the identity of ∗ is 0, so solve 3 + b + 3(3)b = 0.
reciprocal (conceptual): 1/3 (the ordinary inverse) was given; the inverse b must satisfy 3 ∗ b = e, where e = 9 is this operation's identity.

teach.idea: The identity e leaves every element unchanged: a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a. An inverse of a is an element b with a ∗ b = b ∗ a = e. Both depend on the rule, not on ordinary + or ×.
teach.method: Write a ∗ e = a with the rule and solve for e (it must not depend on a). Then write a ∗ b = e with the given a and solve for b.

alternatives.title: Guess and check
text: Try a candidate e with two or three different values of a: if a ∗ e = a every time, e is the identity.
For the inverse, work out a ∗ b with your b: you must get e.

families.title: Is a binary operation commutative, associative, both or neither?
explanations: product-term (conceptual): The rule looked too complicated to be associative; expand (a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) fully: they are the same.
comm-implies-assoc (conceptual): Commutative was taken to mean associative as well; associativity must be checked separately with three elements.
equal-test (procedural): Commutativity was checked with a = b, where it always holds; try two different numbers.
not-comm-not-assoc (conceptual): Because the rule is not commutative it was assumed not associative either; check (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) on its own.

teach.idea: Commutative: a ∗ b = b ∗ a for all a, b. Associative: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c. Either can hold without the other.
teach.method: Swap a and b in the rule and compare. Then work out (a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) in full and compare. One counter-example (with actual numbers) is enough to show a property fails.

alternatives.title: Hunt for a counter-example
text: Try small numbers such as a = 1, b = 2, c = 3.
If the two sides differ, the property fails; if they agree for several choices, prove it with letters.

families.title: Classifying a function as one-one, onto or bijective
explanations: kind-0 (conceptual): A straight line was thought to miss some values; over ℝ every y is reached, at x = (y − 3)/3.
kind-1 (conceptual): x = (y − 3)/3 works over ℝ, but here inputs must be natural numbers: y = 1 has no natural-number input.
kind-2 (conceptual): Only the values y ≥ 3 were thought of; the codomain ℝ also contains values that x² never reaches.
kind-3 (conceptual): A square was assumed never to be onto; the codomain here is [3, ∞), and every y in it is reached. It is not one-one, since f(−1) = f(1).
kind-4 (conceptual): x² was assumed never to be one-one; here the domain is [0, ∞), so no negative inputs: f(x₁) = f(x₂) forces x₁ = x₂.
kind-5 (conceptual): Over ℤ the line 3x + 3 skips integers (it goes up in steps of 3), so it is not onto.
kind-6 (conceptual): x³ was treated like x²; but x³ is strictly increasing, so different inputs give different outputs.
kind-7 (conceptual): The square was assumed to reach every integer; most integers are not of this form.
kind-8 (conceptual): |x − 3| was thought one-one; f(2) = f(4), so it is not.

teach.idea: One-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is an output. Both depend on the domain and codomain, not only on the formula.
teach.method: For one-one, set f(x₁) = f(x₂) and see whether x₁ = x₂ follows. For onto, take any y in the codomain, solve f(x) = y, and check the solution lies in the domain.

alternatives.title: Horizontal lines
text: Draw horizontal lines y = c for c in the codomain.
One-one: no line meets the graph twice. Onto: every such line meets it at least once.

families.title: Testing a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
explanations: reflexive (conceptual): Reflexive needs (a, a) for EVERY a in A; one missing pair is enough to fail.
symmetric (conceptual): Every pair (a, b) needs its reverse (b, a) in R; one pair without its reverse is enough to fail.
transitive (conceptual): A chain such as (a, b), (b, a) needs (a, a) too; check every chain (a, b), (b, c) for (a, c).

teach.idea: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a in A. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
teach.method: Check the three properties one by one: list the (a, a) pairs; pair each element with its reverse; and for each pair (a, b) look for pairs starting with b.

alternatives.title: The relation matrix
text: Write a 3 × 3 table with a 1 in row a, column b when (a, b) ∈ R.
Reflexive: 1s on the diagonal. Symmetric: the table equals its mirror image. Transitive: wherever row a has a 1 in column b, row a must contain every 1 of row b.

families.title: The fewest pairs that make a relation an equivalence relation
explanations: reflexive-only (conceptual): Only the pairs (a, a) were added; an equivalence relation must also be symmetric and transitive.
no-transitive (procedural): Reflexive and symmetric pairs were added, but the pairs that transitivity forces (from chains (a, b), (b, c)) were missed.
unmentioned-elements (conceptual): Elements of A that do not appear in R were forgotten; each still needs its pair (a, a).

teach.idea: The smallest equivalence relation containing R splits A into classes of elements linked by R; within a class every element is related to every element.
teach.method: Join elements that appear together in a pair of R into classes; a class of n elements needs n² pairs; add up, then subtract the pairs R already has.

alternatives.title: Close it step by step
text: Add every (a, a); add the reverse of every pair; then add (a, c) for every chain (a, b), (b, c).
Repeat until nothing new appears, and count what you added.

families.title: The derivative from first principles
explanations: constant-kept (procedural): The constant 4 was kept; in f(x + h) − f(x) it cancels, so it does not appear in f′(x).
only-square (procedural): Only the x² term was worked out; the 5x term gives 5h/h = 5.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was lost: k/(x + h + 5) − k/(x + 5) has numerator −kh.
not-squared (procedural): Only one bracket was kept in the denominator; after cancelling h, both (x + h + q) and (x + q) remain and become (x + q)².
half-lost (procedural): After rationalising, the denominator is √(x + h + q) + √(x + q), which tends to 2√(x + q); the 2 was lost.
cube-expanded-wrongly (prerequisite): (x + h)³ was expanded as x³ + h³; it is x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³.
sin-split (conceptual): sin(4x + 4h) was split as sin 4x + sin 4h; use sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.
cos-sign (recall): cos(A + B) − cos A tends to −sin A × B: the derivative of cos is −sin.
inner-lost (procedural): sin(4h)/h tends to 4, not 1: write it as 4 × sin(4h)/(4h).

teach.idea: f′(x) is the limit of the slope of a chord, [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, as the second point slides towards the first (h → 0).
teach.method: Work out f(x + h) − f(x), simplify so that h is a factor of the top (expand, combine fractions, or rationalise a root), cancel h, then let h → 0.

alternatives.title: Shrink h with numbers
text: Pick x = 1 and work out the chord slope for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
The slopes settle on a value: that is f′(1). The algebra does the same for every x at once.

families.title: Instantaneous velocity from a distance–time formula
explanations: position (conceptual): The distance at that moment was found; velocity is the rate of change of distance, ds/dt.
average (conceptual): The average velocity over the first 5 seconds (s ÷ t) was found; the instantaneous velocity is ds/dt at t = 5.

teach.idea: Velocity is the instantaneous rate of change of distance: the slope of the distance–time graph at that moment, ds/dt.
teach.method: Differentiate s term by term (d/dt tⁿ = n tⁿ⁻¹), then substitute the given time.

alternatives.title: Shrink the time interval
text: Average velocity from t₀ to t₀ + h is [s(t₀ + h) − s(t₀)]/h.
Work it out for h = 0.1 and h = 0.01: it approaches ds/dt at t₀.

families.title: Intervals where a cubic is increasing or decreasing
explanations: leading-sign (conceptual): The negative leading coefficient was ignored: f′ opens downwards, so it is positive between the roots and negative outside them.
root-signs (procedural): The roots of f′ were read with the wrong signs: (x − 3) = 0 gives x = 3.
inside-outside (conceptual): The two kinds of interval were swapped: f′(x) = 6(x − 3)(x − 4) is negative between the roots and positive outside them.
one-piece (procedural): Only one piece was given; f′ has the same sign on (−∞, 3) and on (4, ∞), so both pieces belong to the answer.

teach.idea: f is strictly increasing where f′(x) > 0 and strictly decreasing where f′(x) < 0; the sign of f′ can only change at its roots.
teach.method: Differentiate and factorise f′. Mark the roots on a number line, test one value of x in each part, and collect the parts with the sign you need.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Make a table with columns (−∞, α), (α, β), (β, ∞).
Write the sign of each factor of f′ in each column and multiply the signs.

families.title: The local maximum or minimum value of a cubic
explanations: x-for-value (procedural): The point where it happens (the x value) was given; the question asks for the value f(x) there.
max-min-swapped (conceptual): The two turning points were swapped: f′ changes from − to + at x = 4, which makes it the local minimum.

teach.idea: At a local maximum f′ changes from + to − (f″ < 0 there); at a local minimum from − to + (f″ > 0).
teach.method: Solve f′(x) = 0, decide which root is the maximum and which the minimum (first or second derivative test), then substitute that x into f.

alternatives.title: Second-derivative test
text: f″(x) = 12x − 6(α + β) for these cubics (times the sign of the leading term).
Negative f″ at a root means a local maximum; positive means a local minimum.

families.title: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
explanations: ends-only (conceptual): Only the end points were checked; the turning points inside the interval are candidates too.
turning-only (conceptual): Only the turning points were checked; on a closed interval the end points can give the absolute extreme.

teach.idea: A continuous function on a closed interval has an absolute maximum and minimum, and they occur either at a turning point inside or at an end point.
teach.method: Find the critical points inside [p, q]; evaluate f there and at p and q; the largest value is the absolute maximum, the smallest the absolute minimum.

alternatives.title: A table of candidates
text: List x = p, the critical points inside, and x = q in one row.
Write f(x) under each and circle the largest and the smallest.

families.title: Rates of change of related quantities
explanations: quantity (conceptual): The area (as a multiple of π) was found, not its rate of change.
rate-forgotten (procedural): dA/dr = 2πr was found but not multiplied by dr/dt = 5.
revenue (conceptual): The total revenue R(x) was found; the marginal revenue is its derivative R′(x).
average (conceptual): The revenue per item, R(x)/x, was found; the marginal revenue is R′(x).
