one-term (procedural): Only the change in width was used; the area A = lb changes through both l and b: dA/dt = (dl/dt)b + l(db/dt).
sign (procedural): The length is decreasing, so dl/dt = −5; the minus sign was lost.

teach.idea: If a quantity Q depends on x and x changes with time, then dQ/dt = (dQ/dx) × (dx/dt): the rates are linked by the chain rule.
teach.method: Write the formula linking the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to t, then substitute the values at the moment asked about.

alternatives.title: A small change in time
text: In a short time Δt, x changes by about (dx/dt)Δt.
Q then changes by about (dQ/dx) × (dx/dt)Δt; divide by Δt.

families.title: Areas bounded by a parabola, a cubic or a quadratic and the axis
explanations: half (conceptual): Only the part above the x-axis was found; the parabola is symmetric about the x-axis, so double it.
signed (conceptual): The curve is below the axis for 0 < x < 3; integrating straight through subtracted that part. Split at x = 3 and add the sizes.
from-zero (procedural): The region from x = −4 to 0 was left out.
above-only (procedural): Only the part from x = 3 to 9 (above the axis) was found; the part between 0 and 3 is also bounded by the curve and the axis.

teach.idea: Area is always positive: integrate the height |y| of the region. Where a curve dips below the x-axis, its integral there is negative, so split the interval at the crossing and add the sizes.
teach.method: Sketch the region, find where the curve meets the axis, write the area as a sum of integrals of positive heights (use symmetry where it helps), and evaluate.

alternatives.title: Horizontal strips
text: For y² = 4ax and x = c, take strips parallel to the x-axis: their length is c − y²/(4a).
Integrate from y = −2√(ac) to 2√(ac).

families.title: Choosing k to make a function continuous
explanations: move-sign (prerequisite): 3 was moved across without changing its sign: 3k + 3 = 30 gives 3k = 30 − 3.
no-divide (procedural): The equation 3k + 3 = 30 was not finished: divide by 3.
upside-down (procedural): The ratio was turned over: sin(6x)/(5x) = (6/5) × sin(6x)/(6x), which tends to 6/5.
m-lost (procedural): sin(6x)/x was taken as 1; it tends to 6, since sin θ/θ → 1 needs θ = 6x in both places.
half-lost (procedural): After multiplying by √(1 + mx) + 1, the denominator tends to 2; the 2 was lost.
not-squared (procedural): 1 − cos(6x) = 2 sin²(6x/2), which gives (6x)²/2: the 6 is squared.
cube-factor (prerequisite): x³ − 216 was factorised as (x − 6)(x² + 36); it is (x − 6)(x² + 6x + 36).
zero (conceptual): 0/0 was taken as 0; it means the expression must be simplified (cancel x − u) before substituting.

teach.idea: f is continuous at a when lim (x → a) f(x) exists and equals f(a): the left limit, the right limit and the value all agree.
teach.method: Find the limit of the formula near a (substitute for a polynomial; use sin θ/θ → 1, 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), rationalising or factorising otherwise), then set f(a) equal to it.

alternatives.title: Left value, right value
text: For a function in two pieces, work out each piece at x = a.
Continuity means the two values are equal: that is an equation for k.

families.title: Intervals of concavity of a cubic or quartic
explanations: swapped (conceptual): Upward and downward were swapped: y″ = 6(x − 4) is positive to the right of x = 4, so the curve is concave upward there.
one-piece (procedural): Only one piece was given; y″ > 0 on both outer pieces.
root-sign (procedural): y″ = 0 at x = 4, not −4: the sign was slipped.

teach.idea: A curve is concave upward where y″ > 0 (its slope is increasing) and concave downward where y″ < 0; points of inflection are where y″ changes sign.
teach.method: Differentiate twice, factorise y″, mark its roots on a number line and test the sign of y″ in each part.

alternatives.title: Watch the slope
text: Concave upward means the tangent slope increases as x increases, like a cup.
So check where y′ is increasing: that is where y″ > 0.

families.title: Definite integrals over [−a, a] using odd and even functions
explanations: all-vanish (conceptual): Every term was taken to vanish over a symmetric interval; only the odd part does. The even part kx² + m gives twice its integral from 0 to a.
not-doubled (procedural): The even part was integrated from 0 to a but not doubled: ∫₋ₐᵃ g = 2∫₀ᵃ g for an even g.

teach.idea: If f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0: the areas on the two sides cancel. If f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
teach.method: Split the integrand into its odd part and its even part, drop the odd part, and integrate the even part from 0 to a and double it.

alternatives.title: Substitute x = −t
text: Write ∫₋ₐᵃ f = ∫₋ₐ⁰ f + ∫₀ᵃ f and put x = −t in the first integral.
It becomes ∫₀ᵃ f(−t) dt, which is −∫₀ᵃ f for an odd f and +∫₀ᵃ f for an even f.

families.title: Definite integrals with the property ∫ f(x) dx = ∫ f(a + b − x) dx
explanations: not-halved (procedural): Adding the two forms of I gives 2I = ∫ 1 dx = 6; the last step, dividing by 2, was missed.
sum-of-limits (procedural): ∫ₐᵇ 1 dx = b − a = 6, not a + b.

teach.idea: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx: replacing x by a + b − x runs over the same interval backwards. For g(x)/(g(x) + g(a + b − x)), the two forms add up to 1.
teach.method: Call the integral I, write it again with x replaced by a + b − x, add the two: 2I = ∫ₐᵇ 1 dx = b − a, so I = (b − a)/2.

alternatives.title: Symmetry about the middle
text: At x and at a + b − x (mirror points about (a + b)/2) the integrand's values add up to 1.
So on average the integrand is ½, and the integral is ½ × (b − a).

families.title: Splitting the interval: |x − c| and the greatest integer function
explanations: no-split (conceptual): |x − 5| was integrated as x − 5 all the way; for x < 5 it is 5 − x, so split at x = 5.
right-only (procedural): Only the part from 5 to 6 was found; the part from 2 to 5 also counts.
as-x (conceptual): [x] was integrated as if it were x; [x] is constant on each interval [k, k + 1), so split at the integers.
one-too-many (procedural): The last unit interval was counted up to 6; the pieces are [2, 3), …, [5, 6), with values 2 to 5.

teach.idea: ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫ᶜᵇ f for any c in between. Split where the formula changes: at x = c for |x − c|, at each integer for [x].
teach.method: Find where the integrand changes its formula, split the interval there, write each piece without | | or [ ], integrate each piece and add.

alternatives.title: Count areas
text: |x − c| makes two triangles above the axis: (c − a)²/2 and (b − c)²/2.
[x] makes rectangles of width 1 and heights a, a + 1, …, b − 1 (below the axis when negative).

families.title: Choosing a and b to make a piecewise function differentiable
explanations: slope-without-x (procedural): The slopes were matched as a = 5, forgetting the 2x from x²: the left derivative at x = 3 is 2(3) + a.
sign-slip (procedural): 2(3) + a = 5 was solved as a = 5 + 6; take 6 from both sides.

teach.idea: Differentiable at c means the left and right derivatives at c are equal; this also needs f to be continuous at c (the pieces must meet).
teach.method: Match the slopes of the two pieces at x = c to find a; then match their values at x = c to find b.

alternatives.title: One tangent line
text: The line px + q must be the tangent to the parabola at x = c.
So the parabola must pass through (c, pc + q) with slope p there.

families.title: Separating the variables in an initial value problem
explanations: constant-in-exponent (procedural): ln y = 2x^2 + 2x + C gives C = ln 5, not 5; the constant was put into the exponent as 5.
y-dropped (conceptual): The y on the right was ignored and only (px + q) was integrated; divide by y first: dy/y = (px + q) dx.
constant-dropped (procedural): The constant was dropped; y(1) = 5 gives y = 5x^4.
constant-added-late (procedural): The constant was added after taking exponentials; ln y = p ln x + C gives y = Axᵖ, a constant multiple.

teach.idea: When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, the variables can be separated: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, and each side integrated.
teach.method: Divide by y, integrate both sides (ln y on the left), add one constant, exponentiate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.

alternatives.title: Check by differentiating
text: Differentiate your y and see whether you get the right side of the equation.
Then put in the starting x and check you get the starting y.

families.title: The order and degree of a differential equation
explanations: largest-power (conceptual): The largest power anywhere was taken as the degree; the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative only.
swapped (recall): Order and degree were swapped: the order is how many times y is differentiated in the highest derivative; the degree is that derivative's power.

teach.idea: The order is that of the highest derivative in the equation; the degree (defined when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives) is the power of that highest derivative.
teach.method: Find the derivative with the most dashes (the largest k in dᵏy/dxᵏ): that k is the order. Its power is the degree; powers of lower derivatives do not matter.

alternatives.title: Rewrite with dashes
text: Write dy/dx as y′, d²y/dx² as y″, d³y/dx³ as y‴.
The most dashes give the order; the power on that term gives the degree.

families.title: A linear differential equation with an integrating factor
explanations: constant-dropped (procedural): The constant of integration was dropped; y·x^3 = … + C, and y(1) = −1 fixes C.
q-not-multiplied (procedural): The right side was integrated without multiplying it by the integrating factor x^3: y·(IF) = ∫ Q·(IF) dx.

teach.idea: For dy/dx + Py = Q, multiplying by the integrating factor e^(∫P dx) turns the left side into the derivative of y × IF.
teach.method: Find IF = e^(∫P dx) (here xᵏ), write y × IF = ∫ Q × IF dx + C, divide by IF, and use the initial condition for C.

alternatives.title: See the product rule
text: d/dx (xᵏy) = xᵏ dy/dx + k xᵏ⁻¹ y = xᵏ (dy/dx + (k/x)y).
So multiplying the equation by xᵏ makes the left side d/dx (xᵏy).

families.title: A homogeneous differential equation with y = vx
explanations: constant-dropped (procedural): The constant of integration was dropped (taken as 0); the initial condition fixes it.
dv-for-dy (conceptual): With y = vx, dy/dx was taken as dv/dx; by the product rule dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
two-lost (procedural): ∫ v dv = v²/2; the factor 2 was lost when solving for v².

teach.idea: In a homogeneous equation dy/dx depends only on y/x. Putting y = vx (so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx) turns it into a separable equation in v and x.
teach.method: Substitute y = vx and dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, simplify to x dv/dx = g(v), separate and integrate, put v = y/x back, and use the initial condition.

alternatives.title: Check your answer
text: Differentiate your y and work out the right side of the equation with it.
They must agree, and your y must equal the given value at x = 1.

families.title: Second-order derivatives
explanations: stopped-early (procedural): Only the first derivative was found; d²y/dx² means differentiate once more.
b-squared-sign (recall): The derivative of sin(3x) is +3cos(3x); a sign slip turned −b² into +b².
chain-once (procedural): The chain-rule factor 5 was used only once; each differentiation of (5x + 4) brings a factor 5.
product-once (procedural): Only the eᵃˣ factor was differentiated each time; the product rule also differentiates the x.
x-as-constant (procedural): x was treated as a constant multiplier; x sin ax is a product, so use the product rule.

teach.idea: The second derivative d²y/dx² is the derivative of dy/dx: how fast the slope itself is changing.
teach.method: Differentiate once (product and chain rules), simplify, then differentiate the result again; collect like terms at the end.

alternatives.title: Spot the pattern
text: For eᵃˣ times sin bx or cos bx, each differentiation keeps the factor eᵃˣ and mixes sin and cos.
Write dy/dx = eᵃˣ(…), then differentiate the bracket and the eᵃˣ again.

families.title: The differential equation satisfied by a family of functions
explanations: sign-p (procedural): The sign of p was slipped: the roots r of r² + pr + q = 0 add up to −p.
sign-q (procedural): The sign of q was slipped: the product of the roots is +q.
b-sign (recall): The derivative of cos is −sin; a sign slip turned a² + b² into a² − b².

teach.idea: y = eʳˣ satisfies y″ + py′ + qy = 0 exactly when r² + pr + q = 0. A family with two arbitrary constants comes from the two roots of that quadratic.
teach.method: Read off the roots r₁, r₂ from the exponents (a repeated root for (A + Bx)eᵐˣ, a ± ib for eᵃˣ(A cos bx + B sin bx)); then p = −(r₁ + r₂) and q = r₁r₂.

alternatives.title: Eliminate A and B
text: Write y, y′ and y″ in terms of A and B.
Combine them so that A and B cancel; the coefficients give p and q.

families.title: Implicit differentiation of a second-degree curve
explanations: xy-product-rule (procedural): The term 4xy was differentiated as 4y only; it is a product, so its derivative is 4(y + x dy/dx).
y-terms-no-dydx (conceptual): The y² and y terms were differentiated as if y were x, without the factor dy/dx; y depends on x, so d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was lost when the x-terms were moved to the other side.
upside-down (procedural): The fraction was turned upside down: divide by the bracket that multiplies dy/dx.

teach.idea: y is a function of x, so every y term picks up a factor dy/dx by the chain rule: d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx, and d/dx(xy) = y + x dy/dx.
teach.method: Differentiate both sides term by term with respect to x, move the terms without dy/dx to the other side, factor out dy/dx and divide.

alternatives.title: Use partial derivatives
text: Write the curve as F(x, y) = constant.
Then dy/dx = −F_x / F_y, where F_x treats y as a constant and F_y treats x as a constant.

families.title: dy/dx for a curve given in parametric form
explanations: upside-down (conceptual): dx/dt was divided by dy/dt; dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).
divide-functions (conceptual): y was divided by x without differentiating; dy/dx is the ratio of the two derivatives, not of x and y.
x-not-differentiated (procedural): Only y was differentiated; the derivative of y was divided by x itself instead of by dx/dt.

teach.idea: When x and y both depend on t, a small change in t changes y by (dy/dt)Δt and x by (dx/dt)Δt, so dy/dx = (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).
teach.method: Differentiate x and y with respect to t separately, then divide dy/dt by dx/dt and simplify the powers of t.

alternatives.title: Eliminate t first
text: Write t in terms of x and substitute into y to get y as a function of x.
Differentiate, then write the answer back in terms of t; it agrees with (dy/dt) ÷ (dx/dt).

families.title: Logarithmic differentiation of (ax + b) to the power kx
explanations: power-rule (conceptual): The power rule was used as if the power were a fixed number; here the power depends on x, so take logarithms first.
base-constant (conceptual): The base was treated as a constant (as for aˣ); the base also changes with x, which gives a second term from the product rule.
forgot-y (procedural): After differentiating ln y, the result was not multiplied by y; (1/y) dy/dx = … gives dy/dx = y × (…).

teach.idea: When both the base and the power change with x, neither the power rule nor the rule for aˣ applies; taking ln turns the power into a product, which the product rule can handle.
teach.method: Write ln y = (power) × ln(base), differentiate both sides (the left side gives (1/y) dy/dx), then multiply by y.

alternatives.title: Rewrite as an exponential
text: Write y = e^(kx ln(ax + b)).
Differentiate with the chain rule: y′ = e^(kx ln(ax + b)) × d/dx[kx ln(ax + b)], which is the same answer.

families.title: Indeterminate limits by l'Hôpital's rule
explanations: upside-down (procedural): The limit of the denominator's derivative over the numerator's was taken; keep the numerator on top.
chain-forgotten (procedural): The factor 6 from the chain rule was missed in each derivative.
x2-as-x (procedural): The derivative of x² was taken as x; it is 2x.
cos-sign (recall): The derivative of cos was taken as +sin; it is −sin, so the minus signs cancel.
stopped-early (procedural): After one application the limit of sin(6x)/x was taken as 1; it is 6.
ax-derivative (recall): The derivative of 6^x was taken as 6; it is 6^x ln 6.
log-quotient (recall): ln 6 − ln 5 was written as ln 6 ÷ ln 5; a difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a quotient.
one-to-infinity (conceptual): 1 to any power was taken to be 1; here the base only tends to 1 while the power grows, which is an indeterminate form.
no-exponential (procedural): The limit of ln L was given (12) instead of L itself; L = e^(ln L).
add-for-multiply (procedural): The limit of ln L is 2 × 6, not 2 + 6.
tan-as-x (conceptual): tan 6x was replaced by 6x too early, which gives 0; the difference needs the next term, (6x)³/3.
x3-factor (procedural): The factor 3 from differentiating x³ was lost.

teach.idea: Near x = 0 a 0/0 quotient behaves like the ratio of the rates at which numerator and denominator leave 0, so lim f/g = lim f′/g′ while the form stays 0/0.
teach.method: Check the form; differentiate the numerator and the denominator separately (not the quotient rule) and substitute again; repeat while it is still 0/0. For 1^∞, take ln first and exponentiate at the end.

alternatives.title: Use standard series
text: Replace each function by the start of its series: eᵘ ≈ 1 + u, cos u ≈ 1 − u²/2, tan u ≈ u + u³/3.
Cancel the power of x and let x → 0.

families.title: Estimating a root by linear approximation
explanations: no-half (recall): The derivative of √x was taken as 1/√x; it is 1/(2√x).
derivative-at-x (procedural): The derivative 1/(2√x) was worked out as 1/(2x) at x = 100; √100 = 10.
change-sign (procedural): The change Δx = 9 was used with the wrong sign.
no-square (procedural): The derivative 1/(3x^(2/3)) was worked out as 1/(3∛x); at x = 216 it is 1/(3 × 6²).
no-third (recall): The derivative of ∛x lost its factor 1/3.

teach.idea: Close to a point, a smooth curve is almost its tangent line, so f(x₀ + Δx) ≈ f(x₀) + f′(x₀)Δx.
teach.method: Pick x₀ near the number where f(x₀) is easy (a perfect square or cube), find f′(x₀), and add f′(x₀) × Δx to f(x₀).

alternatives.title: Think in differentials
text: Write y = √x, so dy = dx/(2√x).
With x = x₀ and dx = Δx, dy is the small change in the root; add it to the known root.

families.title: Approximate absolute and percentage errors by differentials
explanations: no-power-factor (recall): The derivative of x² was taken as x¹; it is 2x¹.
side-percentage (conceptual): The percentage error in the side was given; the total surface area grows as the square of the side, so its percentage error is 2 times as large.
relative-not-percent (procedural): The relative error was found but not multiplied by 100 to make a percentage.
surface-six (prerequisite): The surface area of a cube was taken as x²; a cube has 6 faces, so it is 6x².

teach.idea: A small error Δx in the side changes the quantity V by about V′(x)Δx; the percentage error is that change divided by V, times 100.
teach.method: Write V in terms of the side, differentiate, multiply by the error in the side; for a percentage, divide by V and multiply by 100.

alternatives.title: Powers multiply percentage errors
text: If V = c xⁿ, then ΔV/V ≈ n Δx/x.
So the percentage error in V is n times the percentage error in x.

families.title: Solving dy/dx + Py = Q with an integrating factor
explanations: factor-sign (procedural): The exponential in the solution was written as e^(4x); dividing by the integrating factor e^(4x) gives e^(−4x).
constant-not-fitted (procedural): The starting value 3 was used directly as C; C must be found by putting x = 1 into the whole solution.
constant-dropped (conceptual): The constant of integration was left out, so the solution cannot meet the starting condition.
q-not-multiplied (procedural): The right side was integrated without multiplying by the integrating factor x³ first.

teach.idea: Multiplying dy/dx + Py = Q by e^(∫P dx) turns the left side into the derivative of a single product, (IF × y)′, which can be integrated directly.
teach.method: Find IF = e^(∫P dx); write IF × y = ∫ IF × Q dx + C; divide by IF; use the starting value to find C.

alternatives.title: Particular part plus free part
text: Find one simple solution of the full equation (for y′ + ay = b, the constant y = b/a).
Add C times a solution of y′ + Py = 0 (here e^(−ax) or x^(−a)) and choose C to fit the starting value.

families.title: The point c in Lagrange's mean value theorem for a cubic
explanations: not-checked-inside (procedural): Both solutions of the quadratic were given; only values strictly between 3 and 5 count.
midpoint (conceptual): The midpoint of the interval was given; that works for a quadratic, but for a cubic c must be found from f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
no-divide (procedural): f(b) − f(a) was not divided by b − a = 2.

teach.idea: A polynomial is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside, so somewhere inside the tangent is parallel to the chord: f′(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
teach.method: Work out the chord slope, set f′(c) equal to it, solve the quadratic for c, and keep only the values strictly between a and b.

alternatives.title: Parallel tangent picture
text: Draw the chord from (a, f(a)) to (b, f(b)).
Slide a line with the same slope across the graph: where it just touches the curve is a point c.

families.title: Where a cubic is increasing or decreasing
explanations: swapped (conceptual): The decreasing part was given; f is increasing where f′(x) is positive, and here the leading coefficient is negative.
root-signs (procedural): The stationary points were read off the factors with the wrong sign: (x − 4) = 0 gives x = 4.
one-piece (procedural): Only one of the two pieces was given; f′ has the same sign for x < 4 and for x > 5.

teach.idea: f is strictly increasing where f′(x) > 0 and strictly decreasing where f′(x) < 0; f′ can change sign only where it is 0.
teach.method: Differentiate and factor f′; mark its zeros on a number line; test one number in each part to find the sign of f′; read off the parts you need.

alternatives.title: Picture the graph of f′
text: Here f′ is a quadratic: a parabola crossing the x-axis at the two stationary points.
If it opens upwards it is negative between them and positive outside; if it opens downwards, the other way round.

families.title: Limits of functions of two variables (0/0 that simplifies)
explanations: zero-over-zero (conceptual): Substituting gives 0/0, which was read as 0; 0/0 says nothing yet, so simplify first.
factor-k (procedural): The factor x² − 16y² was split as (x − 4y)(x + y); it is (x − 4y)(x + 4y).
dropped-y (procedural): sin(4xy)/x was taken to tend to 4; it is 4y × sin(4xy)/(4xy), and y → 5.
dropped-x (procedural): (e^(4xy) − 1)/y was taken to tend to 4; it is 4x × (eᵘ − 1)/u with u = 4xy, and x → 5.
factor-sign (recall): a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) was used with + ab in the second bracket.

teach.idea: A limit asks what the values approach, not the value at the point; if 0/0 comes from a common factor or a standard limit, removing it leaves a continuous function you can substitute into.
teach.method: Substitute to see the form; factor and cancel, or rewrite with a standard limit such as sin u / u → 1; then substitute the point.

alternatives.title: Check along a few paths
text: Approach the point along two or three different straight lines and watch the values.
If they all head to the same number and the function simplifies to a continuous one, that number is the limit.

families.title: Does a two-variable limit at the origin exist?
explanations: one-path (conceptual): Only one path (an axis) was tried; along an axis the values tend to 0, but along a line y = mx they do not, so the limit does not exist.
other-axis (conceptual): Only the other axis was tried, which gives a non-zero constant; along the first axis the values are 0.

zero-denominator (conceptual): The denominator is 0 at the origin, so it was decided that there is no limit; a limit looks at the values near the point, and here the top shrinks faster than the bottom.

teach.idea: A limit at a point in the plane must be the same along every way of approaching; two paths with different limits prove there is no limit.
teach.method: Try y = mx: if the result depends on m (or blows up), the limit does not exist. If the top has higher degree than the bottom, use polar coordinates to show the values shrink to 0.

alternatives.title: Polar coordinates
text: Put x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
If f becomes rⁿ × (something bounded) with n > 0, the limit is 0; if r cancels and θ is left, the limit does not exist.

families.title: Growth, decay and Newton's law of cooling
explanations: linear-growth (conceptual): The same number was added in each 6 hours; growth proportional to size multiplies by 2 each period, so it is ×2^4.
times-2c (procedural): The number was multiplied by 2 × 4 instead of by 2^4.
periods-off-by-one (procedural): The number of half-lives was miscounted: 120 years is 4 half-lives of 30 years.
divide-2c (procedural): The amount was divided by 2 × 4 instead of by 2^4.

linear-cooling (conceptual): The tea was assumed to lose the same number of degrees in each 10 minutes; it cools faster when it is hotter, so the difference from the room is multiplied by the same fraction each time.
room-ignored (conceptual): The room temperature was ignored; it is the difference T − 35 that shrinks by the same fraction.

teach.idea: dy/dt = ky has solution y = y₀e^(kt): in equal times the quantity is multiplied by the same factor. For cooling it is the difference from the room temperature that behaves this way.
teach.method: Write the solution, use the given data (a doubling time, a half-life, a first reading) to find the factor per period, then raise it to the number of periods.

alternatives.title: A table of periods
text: List the time in steps of one period: 0, T, 2T, …
Each step multiplies the quantity (or the temperature difference) by the same factor; fill in the table to the time you need.

families.title: First partial derivatives of a polynomial in x and y
explanations: other-differentiated (conceptual): The term 3x⁴ was differentiated too; for ∂f/∂y, x is held constant, so that term gives 0.
constant-kept (conceptual): The term 3x⁴ was kept as it is; a constant term has derivative 0.
factor-dropped (procedural): The factor x³ in the first term was dropped; a constant factor stays in the derivative.

teach.idea: ∂f/∂x measures how f changes when only x changes: y is held fixed, so it behaves exactly like a number.
teach.method: Go term by term: a term without the variable gives 0; in a term with the variable, keep the other letters as a constant factor and use the power rule.

alternatives.title: Put a number in for the other letter
text: For ∂f/∂x, imagine y = 2: the function becomes an ordinary function of x.
Differentiate it, then put y back where the 2 was.

families.title: Euler's theorem for a homogeneous polynomial
explanations: forgot-degree (recall): The value of f itself was given; Euler's theorem says x f_x + y f_y = n f, with n = 4 here.
degree-off (recall): The degree was taken as 3; every term here has degree 4.
one-part (procedural): Only x ∂f/∂x was worked out; the y ∂f/∂y part was left out.

teach.idea: If every term of f has degree n, scaling (x, y) by t scales f by tⁿ; differentiating that at t = 1 gives x f_x + y f_y = n f.
teach.method: Check the degree of each term, work out f at the point, and multiply by the degree. (Working out both partial derivatives directly gives the same number.)

alternatives.title: Work it out directly
text: Find f_x and f_y, put in the point, and form x f_x + y f_y.
Compare with n f: they agree, which is Euler's theorem in action.

families.title: Integrating by partial fractions (two linear factors)
explanations: log-of-denominator (conceptual): The answer ln|x² − 7x + 12| was used; that is only right when the top is exactly the derivative of the bottom. Split into partial fractions first.
swapped-constants (procedural): The two partial-fraction constants were attached to the wrong factors.
cover-up-sign (procedural): One partial-fraction constant came out with the wrong sign; check by adding the fractions back together.

teach.idea: A fraction over (x − a)(x − b) is a sum A/(x − a) + B/(x − b), and each of those integrates to a logarithm.
teach.method: Factorise the denominator; find A by covering (x − a) and putting x = a in what is left, and B likewise; integrate to A ln|x − a| + B ln|x − b| + C.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Write px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a).
Match the x terms and the constant terms to get two equations for A and B.

families.title: ∫ sinᵐx cosⁿx over [0, π/2] or [0, π] by reduction formulae
explanations: pi-forgotten (recall): When both powers are even, the reduction ends at ∫ 1 dx over [0, π/2], which is π/2; that factor was left out.
no-doubling (procedural): The value over [0, π/2] was given; over [0, π] the integral is twice that (the graph is symmetric about x = π/2).
pi-added (recall): A factor π/2 was put in; it appears only when both powers are even, and here the reduction ends at ∫ sin x dx or ∫ cos x dx, which is 1.

teach.idea: Integrating by parts once gives a formula that lowers a power by 2: ∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿx dx = ((n − 1)/n) ∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿ⁻²x dx, ending at π/2 (power 0) or 1 (power 1).
teach.method: Multiply the fractions (n − 1)/n, (n − 3)/(n − 2), … down to 1/2 or 2/3; include π/2 only when every power is even. For sinᵐ cosⁿ, the denominators are m + n, m + n − 2, ….

alternatives.title: The double-factorial pattern
text: Write (m − 1)(m − 3)… × (n − 1)(n − 3)… over (m + n)(m + n − 2)…, each down to 1 or 2.
Multiply by π/2 when m and n are both even.

families.title: A coefficient in a Maclaurin series
explanations: no-factorial (recall): The 6! in the denominator was left out.
no-power (procedural): Only 1/6! was given; with u = 3x, the term is (3x)⁶/6!, which includes 3⁶.
log-series (recall): The term was divided by 6 (as in the series for ln(1 + x)) instead of by 6!.
sign-pattern (recall): The series for ln(1 + u) alternates in sign: u − u²/2 + u³/3 − …; this term's sign was missed.
factorial (recall): The term was divided by 6!; the geometric series 1 + u + u² + … has no factorials.
sign-of-a (procedural): The sign of u = −x was dropped before raising it to the power 5.

teach.idea: A Maclaurin series writes f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(0) xⁿ/n!; for standard functions the pattern is known, and replacing x by ax multiplies the xⁿ term by aⁿ.
teach.method: Write the standard series in u, put u = ax, and read off the xᵏ term: a power of a, the right sign, and the right denominator (k! for eˣ, sin, cos; k for ln; none for 1/(1 − u)).

alternatives.title: From the derivatives
text: Differentiate f k times and put x = 0.
Divide by k!: that is the coefficient of xᵏ.

families.title: Volume of a solid of revolution
explanations: no-pi (recall): The factor π was left out: each thin slice is a disc of area πr².
not-squared (conceptual): The radius was integrated instead of its square; a disc's area is πx², so V = π∫x² dy.

teach.idea: Cut the solid into thin discs perpendicular to the axis: a disc of radius r and thickness dx has volume πr² dx, so the volume is π∫ r² dx.
teach.method: Write the radius of a slice in terms of the variable along the axis (y for the x-axis, x for the y-axis), square it, integrate over the range and keep π.

alternatives.title: Cylindrical shells
text: For a rotation about the y-axis, slice the region into thin vertical strips at distance x.
Each strip sweeps a shell of volume 2πx × (height) × dx; add them up: V = 2π∫ x × height dx.

families.title: Improper integrals and the gamma integral
explanations: power-one-short (recall): The power of 2 was taken as 6; the gamma integral gives n!/aⁿ⁺¹, so it is 2⁷.
gamma-shift (recall): Γ(6) = 5! was used; here ∫ xⁿe^(−ax) dx needs Γ(n + 1) = n!.
sign (procedural): The antiderivative was evaluated as (value at the bottom) − (value at the top limit); it is top − bottom, and the top value tends to 0.
lower-limit-ignored (procedural): The lower limit was treated as 1 (or ignored); put x = 4 into the antiderivative.
half-missing (recall): tan⁻¹ x tends to π/2 as x → ∞, not π.
a-missing (recall): ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a); the factor 1/8 was missed.
minus-in-denominator (procedural): The denominator came out as a² − b²; integrating by parts twice gives a² + b².
sin-cos-swapped (recall): The results for sin and cos were swapped: ∫₀^∞ e^(−ax) sin bx dx = b/(a² + b²) and with cos it is a/(a² + b²).

teach.idea: An integral to ∞ means the limit of the integral to b as b → ∞; when the integrand dies away fast enough, that limit is a finite number. The gamma integral Γ(n + 1) = ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−x) dx = n! packages repeated integration by parts.
teach.method: Find the antiderivative (or use Γ(n + 1)/aⁿ⁺¹ for ∫ xⁿe^(−ax)), evaluate from the lower end to b, and let b → ∞.

alternatives.title: Integration by parts, step by step
text: For ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−ax) dx, integrate by parts once: it becomes (n/a) × ∫₀^∞ xⁿ⁻¹e^(−ax) dx.
Repeat down to ∫₀^∞ e^(−ax) dx = 1/a.

families.title: Centre and radius of a circle from its general equation
explanations: centre-sign (procedural): The centre was read with the wrong signs: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f).
constant-sign (procedural): The constant term was added instead of subtracted: r = √(g² + f² − c).
not-divided (procedural): The equation was not divided by 3 first; the x² and y² coefficients must be 1 before reading off g, f and c.
radius-squared (procedural): r² was given instead of r.

teach.idea: Completing the square turns x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 into (x + g)² + (y + f)² = g² + f² − c: a circle with centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
teach.method: Make the x² and y² coefficients 1 by dividing; halve the x and y coefficients to get g and f; the centre is (−g, −f); r = √(g² + f² − c).

alternatives.title: Complete the square directly
text: Group the x terms and the y terms: (x² − 4x) + (y² + 6y) = −c.
Add the squares of half the coefficients to both sides: (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 4 + 9 − c.

families.title: The focus of a parabola
explanations: no-quarter (recall): The number 16 was used as the focal distance; −1616·x means 4a = -16, so a = −4.
wrong-axis (conceptual): The focus was put on the wrong axis; the parabola opens along the y-direction (the variable that is not squared).
vertex-sign (procedural): The vertex was read with the wrong signs: (x − h) means the vertex has x = h.
direction-sign (procedural): The parabola was taken to open the other way; the sign in front of the linear side gives the direction.

teach.idea: y² = 4ax is the set of points as far from the focus (a, 0) as from the directrix x = −a; shifting the vertex to (h, k) shifts the focus by the same amount.
teach.method: Read the vertex (h, k); set the coefficient of the linear bracket equal to 4a; move a from the vertex along the axis (the direction of the unsquared variable, the sign of a giving the way).

alternatives.title: Shift to the origin
text: Put X = x − h and Y = y − k: the equation becomes Y² = 4aX (or X² = 4aY).
Its focus is (a, 0) in X, Y; add (h, k) back.

families.title: Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola
explanations: hyperbola-formula (recall): The hyperbola rule c² = a² + b² was used; for an ellipse c² = a² − b² (and e < 1).
smaller-axis (procedural): c was divided by the semi-minor axis 5; e = c ÷ (semi-major axis 6).
e-squared (procedural): e² was given instead of e.
ellipse-formula (recall): The ellipse rule c² = a² − b² was used; for a hyperbola c² = a² + b².
over-b (procedural): c was divided by b; e = c/a, where a = 6 goes with the x² term (the transverse axis).

teach.idea: Eccentricity e = c/a compares the distance from the centre to a focus with the semi-axis on which the foci lie; for an ellipse c² = a² − b² (e < 1), for a hyperbola c² = a² + b² (e > 1).
teach.method: Write the equation in standard form, decide which axis is the major (or transverse) one, find c² by the right rule, and divide c by that semi-axis.

alternatives.title: Use e² = 1 ∓ b²/a²
text: For an ellipse, e² = 1 − (minor/major)²; for a hyperbola, e² = 1 + (b/a)².
Take the square root at the end.

families.title: Areas bounded by a parabola or an ellipse
explanations: upper-half (procedural): Only the part above the x-axis was found; the parabola is symmetric about the x-axis, so double it.
wrong-order (procedural): The parabola was taken minus the line; between the meeting points the line is on top, so integrate (line − parabola).
line-only (conceptual): The area under the line was found; the area under the parabola must be taken away.
circle-formula (recall): The circle formula πr² was used with r = 6; an ellipse has area πab.
quarter (procedural): Only the first-quadrant part was found; the ellipse has four equal quarters.
whole-ellipse (procedural): The area of the whole ellipse was given; only the first-quadrant quarter was asked for.

teach.idea: An area between curves is ∫ (top − bottom) dx between the points where they meet; symmetry lets you find one part and multiply.
teach.method: Sketch the region, find where the curves meet, write the vertical gap (top minus bottom), integrate between the meeting points, and use symmetry (×2 for a parabola about its axis, ×4 for an ellipse).

alternatives.title: Slice the other way
text: For y² = ux and x = v, slice horizontally: each strip runs from x = y²/u to x = v.
Integrate (v − y²/u) dy from y = −√(uv) to √(uv); it gives the same area.

families.title: Which conic does an equation represent?
families.skill: identifying a conic from its equation
explanations: any-two-squares-ellipse (conceptual): Two squared terms were taken to mean an ellipse; with equal coefficients the curve is a circle (a special ellipse with e = 0), which is the better answer.
linear-as-square (procedural): The single x term was treated like a squared term; only one variable is squared, which makes a parabola.
both-squares-circle (conceptual): Having both x² and y² was taken to mean a circle; a circle needs the x² and y² coefficients to be equal.
sign-ignored (conceptual): The minus sign between the x² and y² terms was missed; opposite signs give a hyperbola, not an ellipse.

teach.idea: For A x² + C y² + D x + E y + F = 0 (no xy term), the squared terms decide the shape: one squared variable gives a parabola, equal coefficients a circle, same signs an ellipse, opposite signs a hyperbola.
teach.method: Look only at the x² and y² coefficients first; then, if you want to be sure, complete the squares to see the standard form.

alternatives.title: Complete the squares
text: Group the x terms and the y terms and complete each square.
Compare with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², (x − h)²/a² ± (y − k)²/b² = 1, or (y − k)² = 4a(x − h).

families.title: The locus of a point whose distances from two points are in a fixed ratio
explanations: ratio-not-squared (procedural): When both sides of PA = 3·PB were squared, 3 was not squared: the condition becomes PA² = 9·PB².
points-swapped (conceptual): The ratio was applied the other way round (PB = 3·PA). Here P is 3 times as far from A as from B.
bracket-sign (prerequisite): A bracket like (x − 5)² was expanded with the wrong sign of the middle term: (x − h)² = x² − 2hx + h².
not-divided (procedural): The equation was not divided by 8, so x² does not have coefficient 1 as asked.

teach.idea: A locus is the set of all points that obey a condition. Writing each distance with the distance formula turns the condition into an equation in x and y.
teach.method: Let P be (x, y). Write PA and PB with the distance formula, square both sides to remove the roots, expand, collect all terms on one side and divide by the coefficient of x².

alternatives.title: Check with a point you know is on the locus
text: The point that divides AB internally in the ratio k : 1 is k times as far from A as from B, so it lies on the locus.
Substitute it into your equation: the left-hand side must be 0. If it is not, look for a squaring or sign slip.

families.title: The locus of a point equidistant from a point and a line
explanations: line-distance-sign (conceptual): The distance from P(x, y) to the line x = −2 is |x − −2| = |x + 2|; it was written with the wrong sign.
bracket-sign (prerequisite): (y − 6)² was expanded with the wrong sign of the middle term: (y − k)² = y² − 2ky + k².
lost-two (procedural): When the x² terms cancel, the x terms give 16x (the 2 from expanding the squares stays); the expression was divided by 8 instead of 16.

teach.idea: Every point of the locus is as far from the point as from the line, so the two distances can be set equal. The curve is a parabola with S as its focus and the line as its directrix.
teach.method: For P(x, y), the distance to S comes from the distance formula and the distance to the line x = h is |x − h|. Square both, set them equal, expand, and make x the subject.

alternatives.title: Check with the vertex
text: The point halfway between S and the line, on the horizontal line through S, is on the locus.
Its y-coordinate is b and its x-coordinate is (a + h)/2: put y = b into your answer and you should get (a + h)/2.

families.title: The slopes of a pair of lines through the origin
explanations: sum-sign (procedural): The sum of the slopes was taken as +(xy coefficient)/(y² coefficient); for y² + 2hxy/b + … the sum of the slopes is −2h/b.
reciprocal-slopes (conceptual): The equation was solved for x/y instead of y/x, which gives the reciprocals of the slopes. Put y = mx and solve for m.

teach.idea: A homogeneous equation ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 factorises into two linear factors through the origin; putting y = mx turns it into a quadratic whose roots are the slopes.
teach.method: Substitute y = mx, divide by x², and solve bm² + 2hm + a = 0. Check: the sum of the slopes is −2h/b and the product is a/b.

alternatives.title: Factorise directly
text: Treat the equation as a quadratic in y and factorise it into (y − m₁x)(y − m₂x) times a number.
Each factor set to zero is one line; read off its slope.

families.title: The angle between a pair of lines through the origin
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The sign was kept; the acute angle has a positive tangent, so take the absolute value.
lost-two (recall): The formula is tan θ = |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|; the 2 was left out.
denominator-sign (recall): With slopes m₁ and m₂, tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; a minus sign was used in the denominator.

teach.idea: For ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 the slopes satisfy m₁ + m₂ = −2h/b and m₁m₂ = a/b, so tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| becomes |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.
teach.method: Read a, h (half the xy coefficient) and b, work out h² − ab, and use tan θ = |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.

alternatives.title: Find the slopes first
text: Put y = mx to get the two slopes.
Use tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| for the acute angle.

families.title: The equation of a line through two points
explanations: slope-upside-down (conceptual): The slope was found as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run, (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
mixed-order (procedural): The subtraction order was mixed (y₂ − y₁ on top but x₁ − x₂ below), which changes the sign of the slope.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted when finding c.

teach.idea: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the slope from the two given points fixes its direction, and either point fixes its position.
teach.method: Find m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and rearrange to y = mx + c.

alternatives.title: Two-point form
text: Write (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
Cross-multiply and make y the subject.

families.title: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The value of ax₀ + by₀ + c was negative and its sign was kept; a distance is never negative, so take the absolute value.
no-square-root (recall): The denominator is √(a² + b²) = √50, not 50.
constant-left-out (procedural): The constant 4 was left out when the point was substituted into ax + by + c.

teach.idea: The shortest way from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. Its length is |ax₀ + by₀ + c| divided by √(a² + b²), the length of the normal vector (a, b).
teach.method: Substitute the point into ax + by + c, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b²). Simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Find the foot of the perpendicular
text: Write the perpendicular line through the point (its slope is the negative reciprocal).
Solve the two equations together to find the foot, then use the distance formula.

families.title: The distance between two parallel lines
explanations: coefficients-not-matched (conceptual): The constants were subtracted before the x and y coefficients were made the same; divide the second equation by 1 first.
no-square-root (recall): The denominator is √(a² + b²) = √41, not 41.
constants-added (procedural): The constants were added; the distance uses the difference |c₁ − c₂| once the coefficients match.

teach.idea: Parallel lines can be written with the same x and y coefficients; then they differ only in the constant, and the gap between them is |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).
teach.method: Divide one equation so the x and y coefficients match the other, then use |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).

alternatives.title: Pick a point on one line
text: Choose any point on the first line, e.g. where it crosses an axis.
Find its perpendicular distance to the second line.

families.title: The angle between two lines in general form
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The sign of (m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂) was kept; the acute angle needs the absolute value.
denominator-sign (recall): The formula is tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; a minus sign was used in the denominator.
slope-is-x-coefficient (conceptual): The x coefficient was taken as the slope; for ax + by + c = 0 the slope is −a/b.

teach.idea: The angle between two lines is the difference of their inclinations, so tan θ = (m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂) from the subtraction formula for tan; the absolute value gives the acute angle.
teach.method: Find each slope as −a/b, then work out |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.

alternatives.title: Use direction vectors
text: The line ax + by + c = 0 runs in the direction (b, −a).
cos θ = |u·v|/(|u||v|) for the two directions, then tan θ = sin θ/cos θ.

families.title: Parallel, perpendicular or neither
explanations: coefficients-must-match (conceptual): The lines were called not parallel because their coefficients differ; a multiple of the same x and y coefficients gives the same slope.
perpendicular-missed (procedural): Only parallel was tested. Also check whether the product of the slopes is −1 (or a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0).
reciprocal-no-sign (conceptual): Slopes that multiply to +1 were taken as perpendicular; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
negative-not-reciprocal (conceptual): Slopes that are negatives of each other were taken as perpendicular; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).

teach.idea: The slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
teach.method: Find both slopes (or test a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0 for parallel and a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0 for perpendicular, which also works for vertical lines).

alternatives.title: Compare the normal vectors
text: (a, b) is perpendicular to the line ax + by + c = 0.
Lines are parallel when their normals are multiples of each other, and perpendicular when the normals have dot product 0.

families.title: The tangent or normal to a circle or parabola at a point
explanations: gave-normal (conceptual): The normal (the line along the radius or perpendicular to the curve) was given; the tangent touches the curve, perpendicular to the normal.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted when finding c.
gave-tangent (conceptual): The tangent was given; the normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the point, so its slope is −1/(tangent slope).
normal-term-lost (procedural): The normal to y² = 4ax at (at², 2at) is y = −tx + 2at + at³; the at³ term (162) was lost.

teach.idea: The tangent at a point has the slope of the curve there (from implicit differentiation or the standard formulas); the normal is perpendicular to it.
teach.method: Circle x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): tangent xx₁ + yy₁ = r². Parabola y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): tangent ty = x + at², normal y = −tx + 2at + at³. Rearrange to y = mx + c.

alternatives.title: Differentiate implicitly
text: Differentiate the curve's equation with respect to x and solve for dy/dx at the point.
That is the tangent slope; the normal slope is −1 divided by it. Then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

families.title: The condition for y = mx + c to be a tangent
explanations: inverted (recall): The condition for y = mx + c to touch y² = 4ax is c = a/m; it was used upside down.
multiplied (recall): The condition is c = a/m, not c = am.
gave-c-squared (procedural): The condition gives c² = 540; the square root was not taken.
lost-one (recall): For the circle x² + y² = r² the condition is c² = r²(1 + m²); the 1 was left out.
axes-swapped (recall): In c² = a²m² + b², a² goes with m² (a² is under x²); the two denominators were swapped.
ellipse-sign (recall): For the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 the condition is c² = a²m² − b²; the ellipse's + sign was used.

teach.idea: A line is a tangent when it meets the conic in exactly one point: substituting y = mx + c gives a quadratic in x whose discriminant is 0.
teach.method: Use the standard conditions: parabola y² = 4ax: c = a/m; circle x² + y² = r²: c² = r²(1 + m²); ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² + b²; hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² − b².

alternatives.title: Use the discriminant
text: Substitute y = mx + c into the conic's equation and collect a quadratic in x.
Set b² − 4ac of that quadratic to 0 and solve for c.

families.title: The distance between two points in space
explanations: no-square-root (procedural): The square root was not taken at the end: the distance is √(sum of the squares).
added-differences (conceptual): The differences were added; in space the straight distance is √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).
added-coordinates (procedural): The coordinates were added instead of subtracted; use (x₂ − x₁), (y₂ − y₁), (z₂ − z₁).

teach.idea: In space, Pythagoras is used twice: across the floor (x and y) and then up (z), giving √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).
teach.method: Subtract the coordinates, square each difference, add, and take the square root. Simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: The diagonal of a box
text: Think of a cuboid with edges |Δx|, |Δy| and |Δz|.
The distance between the points is the space diagonal of that box.

families.title: The point dividing a segment in space in a ratio
explanations: ratio-reversed (procedural): The weights were swapped: for the ratio m : n from A, B is multiplied by m and A by n.
external (conceptual): The formula for external division (with a minus sign) was used; internal division adds the weighted points.
not-divided (procedural): The weighted sum was not divided by m + n = 7.

teach.idea: The point that divides AB in the ratio m : n is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, the same in every coordinate.
teach.method: P = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n)). For the midpoint, m = n = 1.

alternatives.title: Go a fraction of the way
text: Find B − A, the step from A to B.
Add m/(m + n) of that step to A.

families.title: Where a point lies in space: octant, plane or axis
explanations: zero-names-axis (conceptual): A point with z = 0 was placed on the z-axis; z = 0 means the point is in the plane of the other two axes.
sign-ignored (procedural): The negative z-coordinate was read as positive; the sign of each coordinate decides the octant.
axis-or-plane (conceptual): Only x is not zero, so the point is on the x-axis; the yz-plane is where x = 0.

teach.idea: The three coordinate planes (xy, yz, zx) divide space into eight octants. A zero coordinate puts a point on a coordinate plane; two zeros put it on an axis.
teach.method: Count the zero coordinates. None: use the signs of x, y and z to name the octant. One zero (say z = 0): the point is in the plane of the other two axes (the xy-plane). Two zeros: the point is on the remaining axis.

alternatives.title: A corner of a room
text: Stand in the corner of a room: the floor edges are the x- and y-axes, and the vertical edge is the z-axis.
The floor is the xy-plane (z = 0); the two walls are the yz- and zx-planes.

families.title: Direction cosines of the line through two points
explanations: ratios-not-cosines (conceptual): These are direction ratios; direction cosines are the ratios divided by the length √5, so that l² + m² + n² = 1.
reversed (procedural): The direction from B to A was used; from A to B, subtract A from B.
no-square-root (procedural): The ratios were divided by 5 instead of √5.

teach.idea: Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the axes; they are the components of a unit vector along the line, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
teach.method: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), and divide each ratio by it.

alternatives.title: Make a unit vector
text: Write AB as a vector a î + b ĵ + c k̂.
Divide by its magnitude: the components of the unit vector are l, m and n.

families.title: Parallel, intersecting or skew lines
explanations: multiple-not-parallel (conceptual): The direction vectors were called different; one is a multiple of the other, so the lines are parallel.

not-parallel-so-meet (conceptual): In space, lines that are not parallel need not meet; check whether a common point exists by solving for λ and μ (lines that never meet and are not parallel are skew).
one-equation-only (procedural): λ and μ found from two coordinates must also satisfy the third coordinate; here they do, so the lines meet.

teach.idea: In space two lines are parallel (directions are multiples), intersecting (they share a point), or skew (neither: not parallel and never meet).
teach.method: If the directions are multiples, the lines are parallel. Otherwise set the general points equal, solve two of the coordinate equations for λ and μ, and test the third: it holds for intersecting lines and fails for skew lines.

alternatives.title: Use the scalar triple product
text: Non-parallel lines meet exactly when (B − A)·(u × v) = 0, i.e. A, B, u, v lie in one plane.
A non-zero value means the lines are skew.

families.title: The angle between two lines in space
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The dot product was negative and its sign was kept; for the acute angle, take |u·v|.
used-points (conceptual): The position vectors of the points on the lines were used; the angle between lines depends only on their direction vectors (the vectors multiplied by λ and μ).
no-square-root (procedural): The product of the squared lengths was used; divide by |u||v|, the square roots.

teach.idea: The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors; the dot product gives its cosine, and |u·v| gives the acute angle. cos θ = 0 means the lines are perpendicular.
teach.method: Take the direction vectors u and v (the vectors multiplied by λ and μ), and work out cos θ = |u·v|/(|u||v|).

alternatives.title: Use direction cosines
text: Turn each direction vector into direction cosines (l, m, n).
cos θ = |l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂|.

families.title: The foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line in space
explanations: gave-given-point (conceptual): The point on the line that is written in its equation was given; the foot is the point where the perpendicular from P meets the line, found from (PQ)·d = 0.
lambda-sign (procedural): λ came out with the wrong sign when solving (Q − P)·d = 0.
not-divided (procedural): In (Q − P)·d = 0 the λ terms add up to λ|d|² = 4λ; λ was not divided by 4.

teach.idea: The shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to the line, so the foot Q is the point of the line with PQ·d = 0.
teach.method: Write a general point Q = a + λd of the line, form PQ = Q − P, solve PQ·d = 0 for λ, and substitute back.

alternatives.title: Project onto the direction
text: The foot is a + λd with λ = (P − a)·d / |d|²: the projection of AP on the line.
This is the same λ the dot-product equation gives.

families.title: The shortest distance between skew lines
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The scalar (B − A)·(u × v) was negative and its sign was kept; a distance is never negative.
not-divided (procedural): The projection was not divided by |u × v| = √32.
distance-of-points (conceptual): The distance between the two points written in the equations was found; the shortest distance is measured along the common perpendicular u × v.

teach.idea: The shortest segment joining two skew lines is perpendicular to both, so it runs along u × v. Its length is the projection of any joining vector B − A onto u × v.
teach.method: Work out u × v, then d = |(B − A)·(u × v)| / |u × v|.

alternatives.title: Minimise the distance
text: Write general points P = A + λu and Q = B + μv.
Make PQ perpendicular to both u and v (two equations), solve for λ and μ, and find |PQ|.

families.title: The distance between parallel lines in space
explanations: not-divided (procedural): |(B − A) × u| was not divided by |u| = √12.
distance-of-points (conceptual): The distance between the two points written in the equations was found; the gap between parallel lines is measured perpendicular to them.
mixed-directions (procedural): The cross product was taken with one direction (u) but divided by the length of the other ((2, 2, 2)).

teach.idea: For parallel lines the perpendicular gap is the height of the parallelogram formed by B − A and the direction u: area |(B − A) × u| divided by the base |u|.
teach.method: Find B − A, compute (B − A) × u, and divide its length by |u|.

alternatives.title: Use Pythagoras
text: The part of B − A along the lines has length |(B − A)·u|/|u|.
The distance is √(|B − A|² − that length²).

families.title: The distance from a point to a plane
explanations: no-absolute-value (procedural): The value of ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d was negative and its sign was kept; a distance is never negative.
no-square-root (recall): The denominator is √(a² + b² + c²) = √48, not 48.
constant-left-out (procedural): The constant 7 was left out when the point was substituted.

teach.idea: The shortest distance from a point to a plane is along the normal (a, b, c); dividing ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + d by |n| measures it in units of length.
teach.method: Substitute the point into ax + by + cz + d, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b² + c²).

alternatives.title: Walk along the normal
text: The line through the point along (a, b, c) meets the plane at the foot of the perpendicular.
Find that point, then use the distance formula.

families.title: The point where a line meets a plane
explanations: gave-given-point (conceptual): The point written in the line's equation was given; it is not on the plane. Substitute the general point and solve for λ.
lambda-sign (procedural): λ came out with the wrong sign when the linear equation was solved.
constant-part-lost (procedural): Only the λ terms were substituted into the plane; the constant part n·a was left out.

teach.idea: Every point of the line is a + λu for some λ; the meeting point is the one whose coordinates also satisfy the plane's equation.
teach.method: Substitute x, y, z of the general point into the plane, solve the linear equation for λ, and put λ back into the line.

alternatives.title: Use the Cartesian form
text: Write the line as (x − a₁)/u₁ = (y − a₂)/u₂ = (z − a₃)/u₃ = λ.
Then x = a₁ + λu₁ and so on: substitute into the plane.

families.title: The image of a point in a plane
explanations: gave-foot (conceptual): The foot of the perpendicular was given; the image is as far beyond the plane as P is in front of it, so go twice as far.
wrong-direction (procedural): The step along the normal was taken in the wrong direction (away from the plane).

teach.idea: The image Q of P in a plane is on the normal line through P, the same distance on the other side: the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of PQ.
teach.method: Write the line P + λn, find λ where it meets the plane (the foot), then double that λ to reach the image.

alternatives.title: Use the midpoint
text: Let Q = P + λn. The midpoint P + (λ/2)n must satisfy the plane.
Solve that one equation for λ.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing complex numbers
explanations: i-squared-plus (recall): i² was taken as +1; i² = −1, so 6i × 3i = −18.
parts-only (conceptual): Only the real parts and the imaginary parts were multiplied together; every part of one bracket multiplies every part of the other.
divide-parts (conceptual): The real parts and the imaginary parts were divided separately; multiply the top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator instead.
denominator-sign (procedural): (c + di)(c − di) = c² + d² = 40; it was worked out as c² − d².
not-conjugate (procedural): The top was multiplied by −6 − 2i itself instead of its conjugate −6 + 2i.

teach.idea: Complex numbers multiply like brackets in algebra, with i² = −1. Dividing uses the conjugate: (c + di)(c − di) = c² + d² is real.
teach.method: Product: expand, replace i² by −1, collect real and imaginary parts. Quotient: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, then divide each part by c² + d².

alternatives.title: Turn and stretch in the Argand plane
text: Multiplying by c + di stretches by |c + di| and turns by its argument.
Dividing undoes that: shrink by |c + di| and turn back.

families.title: The modulus of a product or quotient of complex numbers
explanations: added-moduli (conceptual): The moduli were added; the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.
no-square-root (procedural): The squares were not square-rooted: |x + iy| = √(x² + y²).
parts-added (recall): The modulus was taken as the sum of the parts; |x + iy| = √(x² + y²), not x + y.
subtracted-moduli (conceptual): The moduli were subtracted; the modulus of a quotient is the quotient of the moduli: |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|.

teach.idea: The modulus is the distance from the origin in the Argand plane. Moduli multiply and divide: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|.
teach.method: Find |z₁| = √(a² + b²) and |z₂| = √(c² + d²), then multiply or divide them and simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Multiply out first
text: Work out z in the form x + iy.
Then |z| = √(x² + y²): the same answer, with more arithmetic.

families.title: Powers of i
explanations: cycle-of-two (recall): The powers of i repeat every 4, not every 2: i, −1, −i, 1, i, …
negative-power (conceptual): i⁻¹ = 1/i¹, which is not the same as i¹; for a negative power, use the remainder of −1 on division by 4 (it is 3), or 1/i = −i.

teach.idea: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and then the pattern repeats, so only the remainder of the power on division by 4 matters.
teach.method: Divide the power by 4 and keep the remainder r (from 0 to 3, also for negative powers); then iⁿ = iʳ.

alternatives.title: Quarter turns
text: Multiplying by i turns a point a quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin.
Four quarter turns bring you back to the start, so count only the leftover turns.

families.title: The square root of a complex number
explanations: imaginary-sign (procedural): The sign of the imaginary part must match the sign of 128 = 2xy; with x positive, y has the sign of the imaginary part of the number.
parts-swapped (procedural): x and y were swapped: x² − y² must equal the real part.
other-root (procedural): This is the other square root; the question asks for the one with a positive real part.

teach.idea: If (x + iy)² = a + bi, then x² − y² = a and 2xy = b; also x² + y² = |a + bi|. Adding and subtracting gives x² and y².
teach.method: Find |a + bi|. Then x² = (|z| + a)/2 and y² = (|z| − a)/2; choose x > 0 and give y the sign that makes 2xy = b.

alternatives.title: Solve the two equations
text: Write x² − y² = a and xy = b/2.
Try whole-number pairs with xy = b/2 until x² − y² = a.

families.title: The principal argument of a complex number
explanations: arctan-quadrant (conceptual): tan⁻¹(y/x) only gives angles between −π/2 and π/2; when the real part is negative, add or subtract π.
not-principal (procedural): The angle was measured from 0 to 2π; the principal argument lies in (−π, π], so subtract 2π.
basic-angle-only (conceptual): The acute angle α with tan α = |y/x| was given; z is not in the first quadrant, so the argument is found from α using the signs of x and y.

teach.idea: The argument is the angle from the positive real axis to the point z in the Argand plane; the principal argument is the one in (−π, π].
teach.method: Find the acute angle α with tan α = |y/x|. Then use the quadrant: first α, second π − α, third −(π − α), fourth −α.

alternatives.title: Sketch the point
text: Plot z in the Argand plane and mark the angle from the positive real axis.
Anticlockwise angles are positive, clockwise ones negative; choose the one between −π and π.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing in polar form
explanations: arguments-multiplied (conceptual): The arguments were divided like the moduli; when complex numbers are divided, arguments are subtracted.
added-moduli (conceptual): The moduli were added; moduli multiply: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|.
not-principal (procedural): The argument was not brought into (−π, π]; add or subtract 2π.
subtracted-wrong-way (procedural): The arguments were subtracted the wrong way round: arg(z₁/z₂) = arg z₁ − arg z₂.

teach.idea: In polar form, multiplying complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments; dividing divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.
teach.method: Multiply (or divide) r₁ and r₂, add (or subtract) the arguments, and bring the result into (−π, π] by adding or subtracting 2π.

alternatives.title: Stretch and turn
text: Multiplying by z₂ stretches by r₂ and turns by arg z₂.
So the turns add up and the stretches multiply.

families.title: The circle described by a condition on |z|
explanations: ratio-not-squared (procedural): When |z − z₁| = 3|z − z₂| was squared, 3 was not squared: it becomes 9|z − z₂|².
centre-at-z1 (conceptual): The circle was taken as centred at 5 + 5i with radius 3; with a ratio of two distances, expand the condition to find the centre.
not-divided (procedural): |3z − w| = 4 means 3|z − w/3| = 4; both the centre and the radius must be divided by 3.
radius-not-divided (procedural): The centre was divided by 3 but the radius was not: the radius is 4/3.
centre-sign (conceptual): |z − w| = r has centre w (not −w): read the centre with the sign it has after the minus.

teach.idea: |z − w| is the distance from z to w in the Argand plane, so |z − w| = r is a circle with centre w and radius r. A ratio of distances (not 1) is also a circle.
teach.method: Write the condition with |z − w| alone: divide out a factor of z first. For |z − z₁| = k|z − z₂|, put z = x + iy, square, expand, and complete the squares.

alternatives.title: Read it as a distance
text: |kz − w| = r means k·|z − w/k| = r.
So z is always r/k away from w/k: that is a circle.

families.title: Powers of a complex number by de Moivre's theorem
explanations: modulus-not-raised (procedural): The modulus 2 must also be raised to the power 12: (r(cos θ + i sin θ))ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
parts-raised (conceptual): Each part was raised to the power separately; (x + iy)ⁿ is not xⁿ + iⁿyⁿ. Use the polar form.
angle-not-multiplied (procedural): The argument must be multiplied by 12 as well: cos 12θ + i sin 12θ.

teach.idea: In polar form, raising to a power raises the modulus to that power and multiplies the argument: (r(cos θ + i sin θ))ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).
teach.method: Write the base as r(cos θ + i sin θ), apply de Moivre's theorem, then evaluate cos nθ and sin nθ exactly.

alternatives.title: Square repeatedly
text: Squaring first keeps the arithmetic small, but de Moivre's theorem is quicker for large powers.

families.title: The nth roots of a complex number
explanations: one-root-only (conceptual): An equation zⁿ = w with n = 6 has 6 different roots; adding 2mπ to the argument before dividing by 6 gives the others.
argument-ignored (procedural): The roots of unity were given; the argument of the right-hand side must also be divided by n.
argument-not-divided (procedural): Only 2mπ was divided by 6; the whole argument (θ + 2mπ) is divided by 6.

teach.idea: zⁿ = w has n roots, all with modulus |w|^(1/n), spaced evenly round a circle: their arguments differ by 2π/n.
teach.method: Write w = R(cos φ + i sin φ). The roots have arguments (φ + 2mπ)/n for m = 0, 1, …, n − 1; bring each into [0, 2π).

alternatives.title: A regular polygon
text: The roots are the corners of a regular n-sided polygon centred at the origin.
Find one root; the others are turns of 2π/n from it.

families.title: The addition rule for two events
explanations: complement-forgotten (procedural): P(A ∪ B) was given; 'neither' is the complement: 1 − P(A ∪ B).
gave-P-A (conceptual): P(A) includes the outcomes where B also happens; take P(A ∩ B) away.
subtracted-P-B (procedural): P(B) was subtracted; only the overlap P(A ∩ B) is removed from P(A).
overlap-not-subtracted (conceptual): P(A) + P(B) counts the outcomes in both events twice; subtract P(A ∩ B) once.
assumed-independent (conceptual): P(A ∩ B) is given; it was replaced by P(A) × P(B), which is only right for independent events.
overlap-not-added-back (conceptual): 1 − P(A) − P(B) removes the overlap twice; add P(A ∩ B) back.
sign-slip (procedural): The rule was rearranged with the wrong signs: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∪ B).

teach.idea: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap A ∩ B twice, so it is taken away once: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). 'Neither' is the complement of A ∪ B.
teach.method: Write the addition rule, put in the values you know, and solve for the one you need; for 'neither' use 1 − P(A ∪ B), and for 'A but not B' use P(A) − P(A ∩ B).

alternatives.title: Fill a Venn diagram
text: Put P(A ∩ B) in the overlap first.
Then A only = P(A) − overlap, B only = P(B) − overlap, and outside = 1 − (all three regions).

families.title: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
explanations: words-swapped (recall): 'Mutually exclusive' means no outcome in common; these events share an outcome, though together they cover every outcome (exhaustive).
cannot-be-both (conceptual): Events can be both: A and its complement have nothing in common and together cover every outcome.
different-means-exclusive (conceptual): Different events are not automatically mutually exclusive; look for an outcome that is in both sets.

teach.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Exhaustive events cover the whole sample space (A ∪ B = S).
teach.method: Find A ∩ B: empty means mutually exclusive. Find A ∪ B: the whole sample space means exhaustive. Each property is checked separately.

alternatives.title: Tick each outcome
text: Write the outcomes 1 to 8 in a row; tick under A and under B.
A column with two ticks: not exclusive. A column with no tick: not exhaustive.

families.title: Bayes' theorem: which source produced it
explanations: shares-ignored (conceptual): The defect rates were compared without the machines' shares; a machine that makes more bolts also makes more of the defective ones. Multiply each rate by the share first.
joint-not-divided (procedural): P(machine and defective) was given; the bolt is known to be defective, so divide by the total probability of a defective bolt.
condition-reversed (conceptual): P(defective | machine B) = 4% was given; the question asks the reverse, P(machine B | defective).

teach.idea: Bayes' theorem reverses a condition: P(source | result) = P(source and result) / P(result), where P(result) adds up over all the sources (total probability).
teach.method: For each source multiply its share by its rate; add these for the total probability; divide the chosen source's product by the total.

alternatives.title: Count 10 000 items
text: Imagine 10 000 items: split them by share, then count the faulty ones from each source.
The answer is the faulty ones from the chosen source divided by all the faulty ones.

families.title: The theorem of total probability
explanations: bags-averaged (conceptual): The two bags are not equally likely: Bag I is used with probability 5/6. Weight each bag's chance of red by the chance of using it.
balls-pooled (conceptual): The balls of both bags were put together; the ball comes from one bag only, chosen by the die.
one-bag-only (procedural): Only the Bag I branch was counted; add the Bag II branch as well.

teach.idea: When an outcome can happen in several separate ways (through Bag I or through Bag II), its probability is the sum over the ways of P(way) × P(outcome | way).
teach.method: Draw a tree: first branch the bag (with the die's probabilities), then the colour. Multiply along each red branch and add.

alternatives.title: Count equally likely cases
text: Imagine many repeats: in 6 throws, f choose Bag I and the rest Bag II.
Scale up so the balls divide evenly, count the red draws, and divide by all the draws.

families.title: Binomial probabilities
explanations: no-combinations (conceptual): pʳqⁿ⁻ʳ is the probability of one particular order; there are 9C7 = 36 orders, so multiply by 36.
one-value-only (conceptual): 'At most 7' includes every value from 0 up to 7, not only X = 7.
boundary-left-out (procedural): X = 7 itself belongs to 'X ≤ 7'; it was left out.
p-q-swapped (procedural): p was raised to the number of failures and q to the number of successes; it is pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ with r successes.

teach.idea: In n independent trials with success probability p, any one order of r successes has probability pʳqⁿ⁻ʳ, and there are nCr such orders.
teach.method: Use P(X = k) = nCk pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ with q = 1 − p. For 'at least' or 'at most', add the values needed, or use 1 minus the complement when that is shorter.

alternatives.title: Count the paths of a tree
text: Each trial branches into success (p) and failure (q).
Every path with r successes has the same probability; count the paths with nCr.

families.title: Mean and variance of a binomial distribution
explanations: variance-np (recall): The variance is npq; the factor q = 1 − p was left out.
variance-np-squared (recall): The variance is npq, not np².
p-q-swapped (procedural): Variance ÷ mean gives q = 1 − p, not p.

teach.idea: A binomial count is a sum of n independent 0–1 trials, each with mean p and variance pq, so the mean is np and the variance is npq.
teach.method: Mean = np, variance = npq with q = 1 − p. Going back: q = variance ÷ mean, p = 1 − q, n = mean ÷ p.

alternatives.title: Start from one trial
text: One trial scores 1 with probability p and 0 with probability q: mean p, variance p − p² = pq.
n independent trials add their means and their variances.

families.title: Probability from a density function
explanations: density-not-area (conceptual): The density values were subtracted, f(5) − f(4); a probability is the AREA under f between 4 and 5, found by integrating.
power-not-divided (procedural): x³ was integrated to x⁴ without dividing by 4.
lower-limit-ignored (procedural): Only P(X ≤ 5) was found; the part below 4 must be taken away.

teach.idea: For a continuous random variable, probability is AREA under the density curve: P(b ≤ X ≤ c) is the integral of f(x) from b to c, and the whole area is 1.
teach.method: Integrate the density from the lower limit to the upper limit (or find F(x) = P(X ≤ x) first), then subtract: F(c) − F(b).

alternatives.title: Find the distribution function first
text: F(x) = ∫ f(t) dt from 0 to x. For f(x) = (n + 1)xⁿ/aⁿ⁺¹ this gives F(x) = (x/a)ⁿ⁺¹.
Check F(a) = 1, then P(b ≤ X ≤ c) = F(c) − F(b).

alternatives.title: See it as an area (when f is a straight line)
text: When f(x) = 2x/a², the graph from 0 to a is a triangle of base a and height 2/a: area 1.
P(X ≤ c) is the smaller triangle with base c and height 2c/a², whose area is c²/a².

families.title: The constant that makes a density function
explanations: lower-limit-ignored (procedural): The integral was taken from 0 instead of from 5; f is 0 below 5.
power-not-divided (procedural): x³ was integrated to x⁴ without dividing by 4.
height-one (conceptual): f(6) was set equal to 1; it is the total AREA under f that must be 1, not its largest value.

teach.idea: A density never gives negative values and the total area under it is exactly 1 (X must take some value).
teach.method: Integrate k xⁿ over the interval where f is not zero, set the result equal to 1 and solve for k.

alternatives.title: Start from the flat case
text: When n = 0, f is a rectangle of width hi − lo, so its height must be 1/(hi − lo).
For k xⁿ the same idea holds: area = k(hiⁿ⁺¹ − loⁿ⁺¹)/(n + 1) = 1.

families.title: Probabilities of independent events
explanations: exclusive-for-independent (conceptual): Independent events were treated as if they cannot happen together; independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
add-for-and (procedural): The probabilities were added; for both of two independent events to happen, multiply them.
no-overlap-taken (procedural): P(A) and P(B) were added without taking away P(A ∩ B), so the outcomes where both happen were counted twice.
union-as-product (conceptual): 'At least one' was worked out as 'both'.
exclusive-complement (procedural): 1 − P(A) − P(B) treats A and B as unable to happen together; for independent events use (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)).
complement-of-both (conceptual): 'Neither' was taken as 'not both', 1 − P(A ∩ B); 'neither' means A does not happen AND B does not happen.
union-for-exactly-one (conceptual): P(A ∪ B) includes the outcomes where both happen; 'exactly one' leaves them out.
one-way-only (procedural): Only 'A but not B' was counted; 'B but not A' is the other way of exactly one happening.

teach.idea: A and B are independent when knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
teach.method: Multiply for 'both'. Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) for 'at least one', complements (1 − P) for 'not', and add the two separate ways for 'exactly one'.

alternatives.title: A 10 by 10 grid
text: Shade 10 × P(A) rows for A and 10 × P(B) columns for B in a 10 by 10 grid of equally likely squares.
Both is the overlap of rows and columns; count the squares you need and divide by 100.

families.title: Independent or mutually exclusive?
explanations: independent-means-apart (conceptual): 'Independent' was taken to mean 'cannot happen together'. That is mutually exclusive; independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
counts-not-probabilities (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was compared with n(A) × n(B); the test uses probabilities: n(A ∩ B)/N against (n(A)/N) × (n(B)/N).

teach.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Independent events have P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Two events that both can happen cannot be both.
teach.method: Count n(A), n(B) and n(A ∩ B). If n(A ∩ B) = 0 they are mutually exclusive. Otherwise compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).
