alternatives.title: Does B change the chance of A?
text: Work out P(A) and P(A | B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(B).
If they are equal, knowing B tells you nothing about A: the events are independent.

families.title: Mean of a discrete random variable
explanations: divided-by-count (procedural): Σ x P(x) was divided by the number of values; the probabilities already do the averaging, so E(X) = Σ x P(x).
plain-average (conceptual): The four values were averaged as if equally likely; each value must be weighted by its probability.

teach.idea: The mean of a random variable is a weighted average: each value counts in proportion to its probability.
teach.method: Multiply each value x by its probability P(x) and add the products: E(X) = Σ x P(x).

alternatives.title: Imagine many trials
text: If the probabilities have denominator T, imagine T trials: value x turns up T × P(x) times.
Add all the results and divide by T: that average is E(X).

families.title: Variance of a discrete random variable
explanations: mean-square-missing (procedural): E(X²) was given as the variance; the square of the mean must be taken away: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
mean-not-squared (procedural): E(X) was taken away instead of [E(X)]².
probabilities-ignored (conceptual): The four values were treated as equally likely; each squared deviation must be weighted by its probability.

teach.idea: The variance measures how far the values spread from the mean, each squared distance weighted by its probability.
teach.method: Find E(X) = Σ x P(x) and E(X²) = Σ x² P(x); then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

alternatives.title: Use deviations from the mean
text: Work out x − E(X) for each value and square it.
Multiply each square by P(x) and add: Var(X) = Σ (x − μ)² P(x).

families.title: The law of total probability (two bags)
explanations: bags-equally-likely (conceptual): The two bags were treated as equally likely; the die chooses Bag I with probability 5/6, not 1/2.
pooled-bags (conceptual): All the balls were put together in one bag; the bag is chosen first, so each bag's chance must be weighted by the chance of choosing it.
one-case-only (procedural): Only the Bag I case was counted; a red ball can also come from Bag II, so add both cases.

teach.idea: When the outcome can come about in separate ways (a partition: Bag I or Bag II), its probability is the sum over the ways of P(way) × P(outcome | way).
teach.method: List the cases, multiply the chance of each case by the chance of red in that case, and add: P(R) = P(E₁)P(R | E₁) + P(E₂)P(R | E₂).

alternatives.title: Draw a tree diagram
text: First branches: the bags, with their probabilities from the die.
Second branches: red or black from each bag. Multiply along each red path and add the paths.

families.title: A statement and its converse
explanations: converse-same-truth (conceptual): The converse was assumed to be true exactly when the statement is; a converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts and must be checked on its own.
one-example (procedural): One example where both parts are true was taken as proof; a general statement needs every case, and one counterexample shows it is false.

teach.idea: The converse of 'if P then Q' is 'if Q then P'. A statement can be true while its converse is false, so each needs its own check.
teach.method: Try to find a counterexample: a case where the 'if' part is true and the 'then' part is false. If none can exist, the statement is true; one counterexample makes it false.

alternatives.title: Think in factors
text: Every multiple of a is a multiple of b exactly when b divides a (6 → 3 works, 3 → 6 does not: 9).
For n² and n: if a has no square factor, every prime of a must already divide n.

families.title: A counterexample to a 'prime for every n' claim
explanations: obvious-factor-not-smallest (procedural): n = 281 makes every term a multiple of 281, so it is a counterexample, but the question asks for the SMALLEST one; check n = 1, 2, 3, … in order.

teach.idea: A claim about EVERY n is false as soon as one n fails; that n is a counterexample. Checking many n that work never proves the claim.
teach.method: Work out the value for n = 1, 2, 3, … in order and test each for a factor (try primes up to its square root). The first value with a factor gives the answer.

alternatives.title: Look for a forced factor
text: When n = c, every term of n² + an + c is a multiple of c, so the value cannot be prime.
That proves the claim false, but a smaller n may already fail: still check from n = 1.

families.title: True rows of a truth table
explanations: or-as-exclusive (conceptual): 'Or' was read as 'one but not both'; in logic A ∨ B is also true when both are true.
biconditional-as-and (conceptual): 'A if and only if B' was taken as true only when both are true; it is also true when both are false.
conditional-as-and (conceptual): 'If A then B' was taken as true only when A and B are both true; it is false ONLY when A is true and B is false.
conditional-reversed (conceptual): The conditional was read backwards (as 'if B then A'); A → B is false only when A is true and B is false.

teach.idea: A truth table lists every combination of truth values; the compound statement's value in each row follows from the connectives: ∧ needs both, ∨ needs at least one, A → B fails only for T → F, A ↔ B needs the same value.
teach.method: Write the 8 rows of p, q, r. Add a column for each negation, then for the bracket, then for the whole statement, and count the T's.

alternatives.title: Count the false rows instead
text: For an outer →, the statement is false only when the bracket is true and the last part is false.
Count those rows and take them away from 8.

families.title: Tautology, contradiction or contingency
explanations: first-row-only (procedural): Only the first row (p and q both true) was checked; a tautology must be true in EVERY row, a contradiction false in every row.
mostly-true (conceptual): A statement true in most rows was called a tautology; even one false row makes it a contingency.

teach.idea: A tautology is true in every row of its truth table, a contradiction is false in every row, and a contingency is true in some rows and false in others.
teach.method: Make the 4-row table for p and q, work out each bracket and then the whole statement, and look at the final column.

alternatives.title: Simplify with laws first
text: Replace A → B by ¬A ∨ B and use De Morgan's laws.
A ∨ ¬A is always true and A ∧ ¬A is always false; if the statement reduces to one of these, it is a tautology or a contradiction.

families.title: Variance of a frequency distribution
explanations: mean-not-squared (procedural): The mean was taken away instead of the square of the mean: σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄².
divide-by-n-minus-1 (conceptual): The sum of squared deviations was divided by N − 1 = 22; for the variance of a distribution divide by N = 23.
divide-by-values (procedural): Σf(x − x̄)² was divided by the number of different values (5) instead of the total frequency N.
frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The frequencies were ignored, as if each value appeared once.

teach.idea: Variance is the mean of the squared distances from the mean; squaring stops positive and negative deviations from cancelling.
teach.method: Find N = Σf, x̄ = Σfx/N and Σfx²/N, then σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄² (or Σf(x − x̄)²/N).

alternatives.title: Step-deviation (shortcut) method
text: Choose an assumed mean A (the middle value) and the gap h between values; let u = (x − A)/h.
Then σ² = h² [Σfu²/N − (Σfu/N)²]: the numbers stay small.

families.title: Standard deviation of raw data (exact)
explanations: variance-given (procedural): The variance was given; the standard deviation is its square root.
divide-by-n-minus-1 (conceptual): The squared deviations were divided by n − 1 = 5; for the standard deviation of these data divide by n = 6.
mean-deviation-given (conceptual): The mean of the distances from the mean (mean deviation) was found; the standard deviation squares the deviations first.

teach.idea: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it is in the same units as the data.
teach.method: Find the mean, the squared deviations (x − x̄)², their mean (the variance), then take the square root and simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Use Σx² instead of deviations
text: σ² = Σx²/n − x̄² avoids fractions in the deviations.
With n = 6: σ = √(6Σx² − (Σx)²)/6.

families.title: Comparing consistency by the coefficient of variation
explanations: higher-mean (conceptual): The higher average was chosen; a higher mean means scoring more, not scoring more steadily.
smaller-sd (conceptual): The smaller standard deviation was chosen; spread must be compared relative to the mean, CV = σ/x̄ × 100.

teach.idea: The coefficient of variation CV = (σ/x̄) × 100 measures spread as a percentage of the mean, so groups with different means can be compared. The smaller CV is the more consistent.
teach.method: Work out CV for each batter, then choose the smaller one.

alternatives.title: Compare without dividing
text: σ₁/x̄₁ < σ₂/x̄₂ exactly when σ₁ × x̄₂ < σ₂ × x̄₁.
Multiply across and compare the two whole numbers.

families.title: Mean deviation about the mean
explanations: signs-kept (conceptual): The deviations x − x̄ were added with their signs, and they always add up to 0; mean deviation uses the distances |x − x̄|.
divide-by-n-minus-1 (procedural): The sum of the distances was divided by 5; divide by the number of values, 6.
about-median (procedural): The distances were measured from the median; this question asks about the mean.

teach.idea: Mean deviation is the average DISTANCE of the values from the mean; distances are never negative, so signs are dropped.
teach.method: Find x̄, write each |x − x̄|, add them and divide by the number of values.

alternatives.title: Use the balance of the mean
text: The deviations above the mean add up to the same amount as those below it.
So M.D. = 2 × (sum of x − x̄ for the values above the mean) ÷ n.

families.title: Mean deviation about the median
explanations: middle-unsorted (procedural): The middle value of the list as written (44) was taken as the median; put the data in order first.
about-mean (procedural): The distances were measured from the mean; this question asks about the median.

teach.idea: The median is the middle value of the ORDERED data; the mean deviation about it is the average distance from it.
teach.method: Sort the data, take the 4th value as the median M, add the distances |x − M| and divide by 7.

alternatives.title: Top half minus bottom half
text: Distances from the median: the three largest values are above M, the three smallest below.
So the sum of distances = (sum of the top three) − (sum of the bottom three).

families.title: Exact values by compound-angle formulas
explanations: distribute (conceptual): tan(A − B) was split as tan A − tan B; tan does not distribute over a sum, so use the compound-angle formula.
formula-sign (recall): The sign in the denominator was wrong: tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B).

teach.idea: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B, cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B, tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B): angles like 75° or 165° come from standard ones.
teach.method: Write down sin and cos (or tan) of each angle, substitute into the formula, multiply out the surds and simplify; rationalise a tan answer.

alternatives.title: Check with the unit circle
text: Locate A ± B on the unit circle: the quadrant tells you the sign of the answer.
For example cos(120° − 45°) = cos 75° must be positive and small (about 0.26).

families.title: Double-angle values from one ratio
explanations: double-the-ratio (conceptual): tan 2A was taken as 2 × tan A; doubling the angle does not double the ratio.
formula-mixed (recall): Two forms of the formula were mixed up: cos 2A = 1 − 2 sin²A = 2 cos²A − 1, not 1 − 2 cos²A.
quadrant-sign (conceptual): sin A was taken as positive; in this quadrant its sign must come from where A lies.

teach.idea: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A, tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan²A); the quadrant fixes the sign of the ratio you work out.
teach.method: Use sin²A + cos²A = 1 to find the other ratio, give it the sign of its quadrant, then substitute into the double-angle formula.

alternatives.title: Draw the reference triangle
text: Sketch a right triangle with the given ratio (for example opposite 3, hypotenuse 5) and find the third side.
Put A in its quadrant: the x-side takes the sign of x there, the y-side the sign of y.

families.title: Products of sines and cosines as sums
explanations: sign-between-terms (recall): The order was reversed: 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B).
halved (procedural): The answer was halved; the factor 2 in front of the product is exactly what the formula 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) uses.
minus-dropped (procedural): The terms were swapped and the result is the negative of the right answer.

teach.idea: Adding sin(A + B) and sin(A − B) cancels the cos A sin B parts and leaves 2 sin A cos B; the other three product formulas come the same way.
teach.method: Pick the formula for the product, put A = ax and B = bx, and write the angles A + B and A − B.

alternatives.title: Derive it from the compound-angle formulas
text: Write cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.
Subtract: cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) = 2 sin A sin B.

families.title: Solutions of a trigonometric equation in 0° ≤ x < 360°
explanations: principal-only (conceptual): Only the principal value was given; tan takes each value once in every 180°, so look in every quadrant where it has this sign.
one-turn-only (procedural): Only angles 3x below 360° were used; when 0° ≤ x < 360°, 3x runs from 0° up to 1080°.

teach.idea: sin and cos repeat every 360° and take each value twice per turn (once for tan, which repeats every 180°); the quadrant signs (All, Sin, Tan, Cos) tell you where.
teach.method: Find the reference angle from the standard values, place it in each quadrant where the function has the right sign, then (for kx) add multiples of 360° until kx passes 360k°, and divide by k.

alternatives.title: Read it off the graph
text: Sketch y = sin x for 0° to 360° and the line y = value.
Each crossing is a solution; for sin kx the graph squeezes k waves into 360°, so there are k times as many crossings.

families.title: General solution of a trigonometric equation
explanations: wrong-pattern (recall): The sine pattern was used for a tangent equation; tan y = tan α gives y = nπ + α, because tan repeats every π.
one-family-only (conceptual): Only every 2π was counted; tan repeats every π, so the solutions come every π (divided by the multiple of x).

teach.idea: sin y = sin α ⇔ y = nπ + (−1)ⁿα; cos y = cos α ⇔ y = 2nπ ± α; tan y = tan α ⇔ y = nπ + α (n any integer), with α the principal value.
teach.method: Write the right side as f(α) using the principal value, apply the matching general form to kx, then divide everything by k.

alternatives.title: List and check a few solutions
text: Put n = 0, 1, 2, −1 into an option and check each angle in the equation.
Also find the solutions in one turn from the quadrants: the right option must give all of them and nothing else.

families.title: Trigonometric functions of any angle
explanations: quadrant-sign (conceptual): The sign was wrong: in the quadrant of 1050°, cot is negative.
negative-ignored (conceptual): cot(−30°) was worked out as cot 30°; a negative angle is measured clockwise (sin, tan, cosec, cot change sign; cos and sec do not).

no-cofunction-change (procedural): The angle was written as a multiple of 90° plus 60°, but cot was kept; after an ODD multiple of 90° the function changes to its co-function (sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot, sec ↔ cosec).

teach.idea: Every angle has the same trigonometric values as its position on the unit circle; the value is the reference angle's value with the sign of the quadrant (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).
teach.method: Add or take away 360° until the angle is between 0° and 360°, find its reference angle (its distance from the x-axis), then attach the sign of the function in that quadrant.

alternatives.title: Allied-angle rules
text: Write the angle as 90° × n ± θ.
If n is even keep the function; if n is odd change to its co-function. Then fix the sign from the quadrant of the original angle.

families.title: The period of a trigonometric function
explanations: multiply-not-divide (procedural): The period was multiplied by the number in front of x; a bigger multiple of x makes the graph repeat SOONER, so divide.
period-mixed (recall): cot repeats every π, not every 2π.

teach.idea: sin, cos, sec and cosec repeat every 2π; tan and cot every π. Replacing x by kx makes the graph repeat k times as fast; the number in front and the shift inside do not change the period.
teach.method: Take the basic period (2π or π) and divide it by k.

alternatives.title: When does the inside complete a cycle?
text: The inside kx + c must grow by one basic period (2π or π).
kx grows by 2π when x grows by 2π/k: that is the period.

families.title: Degrees to radians
explanations: pi-dropped (procedural): The π was left out; 180° is π radians, so the answer is a fraction OF π.
factor-flipped (recall): The angle was multiplied by 180/π; to change degrees to radians multiply by π/180.
full-turn-as-pi (conceptual): A full turn was taken as π radians; a full turn is 2π radians, and π is a half turn (180°).

teach.idea: One radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius; a half turn, 180°, is π radians.
teach.method: Multiply the angle in degrees by π/180 and simplify the fraction.

families.title: Radians to degrees
explanations: denominator-dropped (procedural): π was replaced by 180° but the division by 5 was forgotten.
pi-as-full-turn (conceptual): π was replaced by 360°; π radians is a half turn, 180°.

teach.idea: π radians is 180°, so 1 radian = 180°/π (about 57.3°).
teach.method: Multiply by 180/π; with π in the angle, simply replace π by 180° and simplify.

alternatives.title: As a fraction of a half turn
text: kπ/d radians is k/d of a half turn.
So it is (k/d) × 180°.

families.title: Arc length and sector area
explanations: degrees-used (conceptual): The angle in degrees was multiplied by the radius; l = rθ needs θ in radians.
area-formula (recall): The sector-area formula ½r²θ was used; the arc length is rθ.
inverted (procedural): r was divided by l; from l = rθ, θ = l ÷ r.
multiplied (procedural): l and r were multiplied; θ = l ÷ r.
half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; the sector area is ½r²θ.
radius-not-squared (recall): r was not squared; the sector area is ½r²θ.

teach.idea: With θ in radians, the arc is θ radii long (l = rθ) and the sector is the fraction θ/2π of the circle (A = ½r²θ).
teach.method: Change degrees to radians first (× π/180), then use l = rθ or A = ½r²θ; to find θ use θ = l/r.

alternatives.title: Fraction of the whole circle
text: An angle of x° is x/360 of a full turn.
So the arc is (x/360) × 2πr and the sector is (x/360) × πr².

families.title: Finding a side with the sine rule
explanations: ratio-inverted (procedural): The sines were the wrong way up; a/sin A = b/sin B gives b = a sin B / sin A.
angles-proportional (conceptual): The sides were taken in the same ratio as the angles; sides are in the ratio of the SINES of the opposite angles.

teach.idea: In any triangle a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C: each side is proportional to the sine of the angle opposite it.
teach.method: Write a/sin A = b/sin B, put in the known values and solve for b; then simplify the surds.

alternatives.title: Drop a perpendicular
text: The height from C to AB equals b sin A and also a sin B.
So b sin A = a sin B, which is the sine rule.

families.title: The cosine of an angle from three sides
explanations: wrong-sign (recall): The squares were combined the wrong way; cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc), with the side opposite A taken away.
two-dropped (recall): The 2 in the denominator was left out: cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
wrong-angle (procedural): The formula for a different angle was used; for A, the side a (opposite A) is the one taken away.

teach.idea: The cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A extends Pythagoras: the extra term corrects for A not being 90°.
teach.method: Rearrange to cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc) and substitute; a negative answer means A is obtuse.

alternatives.title: Use coordinates
text: Put A at the origin and AB along the x-axis: B = (c, 0), C = (b cos A, b sin A).
Then a² = (b cos A − c)² + (b sin A)² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.

families.title: Area of a triangle from two sides and the included angle
explanations: half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; the area is ½ab sin C (ab sin C is the parallelogram).
cos-for-sin (recall): cos C was used; the height of the triangle on side b is a sin C, so the area uses sin C.

teach.idea: Taking b as the base, the height is a sin C, so the area is ½ × b × a sin C.
teach.method: Multiply the two sides, multiply by sin of the angle between them, and halve.

alternatives.title: Check with Heron's formula
text: Find the third side with the cosine rule.
Then area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s half the perimeter.

families.title: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions
explanations: outside-branch (conceptual): An angle outside the principal range was given for cosec⁻¹ of a negative number; its principal value lies between −π/2 and π/2, so it is negative here.
odd-rule-misused (conceptual): sec⁻¹(−x) was taken as −sec⁻¹(x); for cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ the rule is π − sec⁻¹(x), because their principal values lie between 0 and π.

teach.idea: Each inverse function returns one angle from its principal range: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹ in [0, π]. That is why it has a single value.
teach.method: Find the standard angle whose ratio is the argument, then make sure it lies in the principal range: for a negative argument use −θ (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) or π − θ (cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cot⁻¹).

alternatives.title: Turn sec⁻¹, cosec⁻¹, cot⁻¹ into the basic three
text: sec⁻¹ x = cos⁻¹(1/x) and cosec⁻¹ x = sin⁻¹(1/x).
cot⁻¹ x = tan⁻¹(1/x) for x > 0, and π + tan⁻¹(1/x) for x < 0.

families.title: sin⁻¹(sin θ), cos⁻¹(cos θ) and tan⁻¹(tan θ)
explanations: cancel (conceptual): The inverse and the function were 'cancelled'; tan⁻¹(tan θ) = θ only when θ is in the principal range.
shift-no-reflect (procedural): A multiple of 2π was removed, but the angle was not brought into [0, π]: use cos(2π − θ) = cos θ.
period-2pi (recall): Multiples of 2π were removed; tan repeats every π, so remove multiples of π.

teach.idea: sin⁻¹(sin θ) is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with the same sine as θ; it equals θ only when θ is already in that range (similarly [0, π] for cos⁻¹ and (−π/2, π/2) for tan⁻¹).
teach.method: Find an angle in the principal range with the same ratio: use sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(2π − θ) = cos θ, tan(θ − π) = tan θ, and add or remove whole turns.

alternatives.title: Use the unit circle
text: Mark θ on the unit circle. For sine, move to the point with the same height on the right half.
For cosine, move to the point with the same x on the upper half; for tangent, to the same line through the origin on the right half.

families.title: Linear combinations of vectors in components
explanations: scalar-first-only (procedural): The number in front of a vector was multiplied into its first component only; it multiplies every component.
minus-first-only (procedural): The minus sign before 3b was applied to its first component only; it changes the sign of every component.

teach.idea: Vectors in î, ĵ, k̂ form are added and scaled component by component, because î, ĵ and k̂ point in independent directions.
teach.method: Multiply every component of a by p and every component of b by q, then add the matching components.

alternatives.title: Write them as columns
text: Write each vector as a column of three numbers.
Scale each column, then add across each row.

families.title: Magnitude of the vector joining two points
explanations: root-missing (procedural): The square root was not taken; |AB| = √(x² + y² + z²).
added-points (conceptual): The position vectors were added; the vector AB is (position of B) − (position of A).
components-added (conceptual): The components were added without squaring; the length comes from Pythagoras in three dimensions.

teach.idea: The vector AB is OB − OA; its length is √(x² + y² + z²), Pythagoras used twice.
teach.method: Subtract A's components from B's, square the three differences, add, and take the square root (simplify the surd).

alternatives.title: The diagonal of a box
text: The differences are the edges of a box with A and B at opposite corners.
The floor diagonal is √(x² + y²); with the height z, the full diagonal is √(x² + y² + z²).

families.title: The section formula with position vectors
explanations: ratio-swapped (procedural): The ratio was used the wrong way round; for 2 : 3 from P, multiply q by 2 and p by 3.
external-as-internal (conceptual): The internal formula was used; for external division R lies outside PQ and r = (mq − np)/(m − n).
internal-as-external (conceptual): The external formula was used; for internal division r = (mq + np)/(m + n).

teach.idea: R divides PQ in m : n internally when PR : RQ = m : n with R between P and Q; then r = (mq + np)/(m + n). Externally, R is outside the segment and r = (mq − np)/(m − n).
teach.method: Choose the formula, multiply q by m and p by n, add (or subtract), and divide each component by m + n (or m − n).

alternatives.title: Walk along the segment
text: Internally, R is m/(m + n) of the way from P to Q: r = p + (m/(m + n))(q − p).
Externally, R = p + (m/(m − n))(q − p), which goes past Q (or behind P).

families.title: Direction cosines of a vector joining two points
explanations: ratios-given (conceptual): The direction ratios (the components of AB) were given; direction cosines are the components divided by the length |AB|.
reversed (procedural): The vector BA was used; AB is (B − A), and reversing it changes every sign.
divided-by-sum (conceptual): The components were divided by their sum; divide by the length √(a² + b² + c²), so that l² + m² + n² = 1.

teach.idea: The direction cosines (l, m, n) of a vector are the cosines of the angles it makes with the x-, y- and z-axes; they are the components of the unit vector, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
teach.method: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), divide each ratio by it and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Think of the angles
text: The angle α with the x-axis has cos α = (x-component)/(length), as in a right triangle.
Do the same for the y- and z-axes.

families.title: The angle between two vectors (cos θ)
explanations: dot-only (conceptual): Only a · b was found; cos θ = a · b / (|a| |b|), so divide by both lengths.
one-length (procedural): a · b was divided by |a| only; that is the projection of b on a. Divide by |a| |b|.

teach.idea: a · b = |a| |b| cos θ, and a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃; together they give the angle. a · b = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
teach.method: Multiply matching components and add (a · b), find |a| and |b|, then cos θ = a · b/(|a| |b|); rationalise.

alternatives.title: Use the cosine rule
text: a, b and a − b form a triangle with sides |a|, |b| and |a − b|.
cos θ = (|a|² + |b|² − |a − b|²)/(2|a||b|), the same as the dot-product formula.

families.title: Projection of one vector on another
explanations: wrong-length (procedural): a · b was divided by |a|; that is the projection of b on a. The projection on b divides by |b|.
dot-only (conceptual): Only a · b was found; the projection is a · b/|b|.
length-squared (procedural): a · b was divided by |b|²; that number scales b to give the projection VECTOR. The projection (a length) is a · b/|b|.

teach.idea: The projection of a on b is the length of a's shadow on the line of b: |a| cos θ = a · b/|b|. It is negative when the angle is obtuse.
teach.method: Find a · b and |b|, divide, and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Dot with the unit vector
text: Make b into a unit vector b̂ = b/|b|.
The projection is a · b̂.

families.title: The cross product in components
explanations: middle-sign (procedural): The ĵ component's minus sign was forgotten when expanding the determinant; the middle term is −(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁).
order-reversed (conceptual): b × a was found; the cross product changes sign when the order changes: a × b = −(b × a).
componentwise (conceptual): Matching components were multiplied; that is part of the dot product. The cross product uses the determinant.

teach.idea: a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b (right-hand rule), with length |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram on a and b.
teach.method: Expand the determinant with rows (î ĵ k̂), (a₁ a₂ a₃), (b₁ b₂ b₃): î(a₂b₃ − a₃b₂) − ĵ(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁) + k̂(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).

alternatives.title: The cyclic pattern
text: x: a₂b₃ − a₃b₂; y: a₃b₁ − a₁b₃; z: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ (follow 1 → 2 → 3 → 1).
Check: the answer dotted with a, and with b, must give 0.

families.title: Area of a triangle by the cross product
explanations: half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; |AB × AC| is the area of the parallelogram, and the triangle is half of it.
root-missing (procedural): The square root of |AB × AC|² was not taken.

teach.idea: |AB × AC| = |AB||AC| sin A is the area of the parallelogram on AB and AC; the triangle is half of it.
teach.method: Find AB and AC, their cross product, its length, and halve it.

alternatives.title: Check with Heron's formula
text: Find the three side lengths with the distance formula.
Area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where s is half the perimeter.

families.title: The scalar triple product
explanations: middle-sign (procedural): The middle term of the expansion was added; the signs go +, −, + along the first row.
order-swapped (conceptual): Two of the vectors were swapped ([b a c]); swapping two rows changes the sign of the triple product.

teach.idea: [a b c] = a · (b × c) is the determinant with rows a, b, c; its size is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c, and it is 0 exactly when they are coplanar.
teach.method: Write the 3 × 3 determinant and expand along the first row with signs +, −, +.

alternatives.title: Cross first, then dot
text: Work out b × c as a vector.
Then dot it with a: multiply matching components and add.

families.title: Coplanar vectors: find λ
explanations: sign-slip (procedural): A sign slipped when solving the linear equation for λ; check by putting λ back into the determinant.
perpendicular-for-coplanar (conceptual): a · c = 0 was used (a perpendicular to c); coplanar means [a b c] = 0.

teach.idea: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when the parallelepiped they make is flat: [a b c] = 0.
teach.method: Write the determinant with rows a, b, c (λ in it), expand to get an expression in λ, set it equal to 0 and solve.

alternatives.title: c as a combination of a and b
text: Coplanar means c = xa + yb for some numbers x, y.
Find x and y from the î and ĵ components; the k̂ component then gives λ.

families.title: The vector triple product a × (b × c)
explanations: terms-swapped (recall): The two terms were swapped: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.
bracket-moved (conceptual): (a × b) × c was found; the cross product is not associative, so the bracket matters.

teach.idea: a × (b × c) is perpendicular to b × c, so it lies in the plane of b and c: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.
teach.method: Work out the two dot products a · c and a · b, then form (a · c)b − (a · b)c component by component.

alternatives.title: Two cross products
text: Find b × c first.
Then cross a with that result; the answers agree.
